py.u01.title: Open the story
py.u01.description: Give your adventure a setting and a surprise.
py.u01.learnTitle: Your story starts with one instruction
py.u01.learn: A program is a set of instructions. Python follows these instructions from top to bottom. Use print() to display words on the screen.
py.u01.detail: Put text inside matching quotation marks, then put that string inside the parentheses. Use lowercase print. The quotation marks do not appear in the output.
py.u01.example:
print("You arrive at a moonlit castle.")
print("A tiny dragon opens the gate.")
py.u01.exampleOutput:
You arrive at a moonlit castle.
A tiny dragon opens the gate.
py.u01.exampleNote: Each print() adds a new line. Two instructions give you two lines of story.
py.u01.question: Which message appears first?
py.u01.why: Python runs the first print statement before the second. Swapping the code lines swaps the messages.
py.u01.guided: Change the dragon into a different creature. Keep the matching quotes and parentheses, then run your story.
py.u01.starter:
# Describe a location with print()
# On the next line, print an unexpected event
py.u01.challenge: Write two print statements with two different story messages: first a place, then a surprise. The check makes sure you print two different messages that use words; whether they make a good scene is up to you.
hints: You need two print() lines: the first describes a place, the second something unexpected.
Check each line: lowercase print, then parentheses, with your message inside matching quotes.
A pattern to complete: print("You wake up in ___.") Then add a second print() with your surprise.

errorHints.text: Every opening quote needs a closing quote, and every ( needs a ). Check the end of each line.
print is all lowercase, and words need quotes around them. Without quotes, Python reads words as names.
Each message needs words, like the name of a place or something that happens.
Keep your first line as it is, and make the second one about something else that happens.

similarExample.code: print("The shop opens at nine.")
similarExample.note: One print() shows one line of text. Your challenge uses two, with your own words.

py.u01.title: Create your hero
py.u01.description: Give the adventure a hero and a useful tool.
py.u01.learnTitle: Remember a detail with a variable
py.u01.learn: A variable is a name that refers to a value. Write hero = "Nova" to store a name. Later, use hero without quotes to read the value.
py.u01.detail: The equals sign assigns a value; it does not print anything. print("hero") displays the word hero. print(hero) displays the value stored under that name. Define a variable before you use it.
py.u01.exampleNote: Changing the two assignments updates the character details without changing the print instructions.
py.u01.question: What does print(hero) display after hero = "Nova"?
py.u01.why: Without quotes, hero means “use the value stored in this variable.” That value is the string Nova.
py.u01.guided: Change Nova to your hero’s name and lantern to a tool of your choice. Run the code to see both values.
py.u01.starter:
hero = ""
tool = ""
# Print hero and tool, using the variables
py.u01.challenge: Store a nonempty hero name in hero and a nonempty tool in tool. Print both values by using the variables. You may add labels or combine them into a sentence.
hints: This card needs two variables, hero and tool, each holding some text. Then print() shows them.
Look at the first two lines: put your own words between the empty quotes. Then check your print(): a variable name goes inside it with no quotes.
With other names: pet = "___" stores text, and print(pet) shows it. Do the same with hero and tool.

errorHints.text: Names must be spelled exactly the same each time: hero in print() must match hero where you gave it a value, letter for letter.
Text values need matching quotes, like "Kai". Variable names inside print() do not.
If your output shows the words hero and tool instead of your values, remove the quotes around the names inside print().

similarExample.code:
pet = "Biscuit"
bed = "rug"
print(pet + " sleeps on the " + bed)
similarExample.note: Two variables hold text, and print() shows their values by name. Your challenge does the same with hero and tool.

otherWays.code:
hero = "Kai"
tool = "rope"
print(f"{hero} packs a {tool}.")
otherWays.note: An f-string puts the values straight into the sentence.

otherWays.code:
hero = "Kai"
tool = "rope"
print(hero, "has a", tool)
otherWays.note: print() can take several values separated by commas, and puts a space between them.

py.u01.title: Meet the player
py.u01.description: Let someone else name the hero.
py.u01.learn: input("What is your name? ") displays a prompt and returns the text the player types. Store that returned text in a variable so your story can use it.
py.u01.detail: Here, player = input(...) saves the response. A plus sign joins strings: "Welcome, " + player. In this academy, fill in Player replies before running; Python reads those replies in order.
py.u01.example:
player = input("What is your name? ")
print("Welcome, " + player + "!")
py.u01.exampleNote: With Nova as the player reply, the welcome includes Nova. Try a different reply and the story changes.
py.u01.question: If the player replies Kai, what will the example display?
py.u01.why: input() returns Kai. The variable player remembers that text, and print() joins it to the greeting.
py.u01.guided: Change the welcome message. Run once with Nova as the reply, then change the reply to Kai and run again.
py.u01.starter:
player = input("What is your name? ")
# Print a welcome that uses player
py.u01.challenge: Ask for the player’s name with input(), store the reply, and print a greeting that includes that reply. It should work for different names without editing the code.
hints: input() gives back whatever the player typed. The starter already keeps it in the variable player.
Look at the comment line: replace it with a print() that joins a greeting and player.
With other names: print("Good morning, " + friend) greets whatever is stored in friend. An f-string works too: f"See you soon, {friend}".

errorHints.text: The reply is stored in player. Check that the name inside your print() is spelled exactly the same.
A name typed straight into the greeting stays the same for every player. Use the variable player in the greeting instead.

similarExample.code:
friend = "Sam"
print("See you soon, " + friend)
similarExample.note: A variable inside a greeting. In your challenge, the value comes from input() instead of being typed into the code.

otherWays.code:
player = input("What is your name? ")
print(f"Welcome, {player}!")
otherWays.note: An f-string puts the reply straight into the greeting.

otherWays.code:
player = input("What is your name? ")
print("Welcome,", player)
otherWays.note: print() with a comma adds the space for you.

py.u01.title: Choose a path
py.u01.description: Make the story respond to a choice.
py.u01.learnTitle: Give your story two possible paths
py.u01.learn: An if statement runs an indented block only when its condition is true. == compares two values. An else block runs when that condition is false.
py.u01.detail: Use a colon after the if condition and after else. Indent the instructions inside each block by four spaces. Our example compares exact lowercase text: left. Any other reply takes the else path.
py.u01.exampleNote: With left as the reply, only the waterfall line runs. With right, only the library line runs.
py.u01.question: Which block runs when path is "right"?
py.u01.why: "right" == "left" is false, so Python skips the if block and runs the else block.
py.u01.guided: Give both paths new discoveries. Run with left, then with right. Confirm that the discoveries differ.
py.u01.starter:
path = input("Left or right? ")
if path == "left":
    # Print one discovery
    pass
else:
    # Print a different discovery
    pass
py.u01.challenge: Ask the player to choose left or right. Use if and else to print a different nonempty discovery for each choice. Keep the replies as lowercase left and right; invent your own discoveries.
hints: You need two branches: one when the reply is left, and one for anything else.
Look at the two pass lines in the starter. Each one is the place for a print() with a discovery.
A pattern from another story: if answer == "yes": then an indented print(...), then else: and another indented print(...).

errorHints.text: Lines inside if and else start with four spaces. Press Tab at the start of the line to add them.
The if and else lines end with a colon, and comparing uses two equals signs: ==.
Your two branches print the same thing. Change the words in one of them.

similarExample.note: One reply, two branches, a different message in each. Your challenge compares the reply with "left".

otherWays.note: != means "is not equal to", so the branches can be written the other way round.

py.u01.title: Launch your adventure
py.u01.description: Bring a player, a setting, and a choice into one small game.
py.u01.learnTitle: Connect the pieces into a game
py.u01.learn: You now know how to display a scene, store a value, ask for input, and choose a path. Combine them in order: set the scene, ask for a name, ask for a direction, then reveal an ending.
py.u01.detail: Keep each input response in its own variable. Use the player’s name in a printed message. Then use if/else to give left and right different endings. Test both paths before sharing your game.
py.u01.example:
print("A floating island appears.")
hero = input("Your name? ")
print("Welcome aboard, " + hero)
path = input("Left or right? ")
if path == "left":
    print("You befriend a cloud dragon.")
else:
    print("You discover a sky garden.")
py.u01.exampleOutput:
A floating island appears.
Welcome aboard, Nova
You befriend a cloud dragon.
py.u01.exampleNote: The same code welcomes different players and produces two endings. That is your first interactive adventure.
py.u01.question: What should you test before sharing the adventure?
py.u01.why: Different replies exercise different behavior. Testing names and both paths catches mistakes a single run might miss.
py.u01.guided: Remix the floating island into your own world. Change both endings and try different player replies.
py.u01.starter:
# Print your opening scene
hero = input("Your name? ")
# Welcome your hero by name
path = input("Left or right? ")
# Use if/else for two different endings
py.u01.challenge: Build your own adventure. Print an opening scene, ask for a name and welcome that player, then ask for left or right and use if/else for different endings. Your story words are up to you.
hints: Four parts, in order: an opening scene, a welcome that uses the name, the path question, and two different endings.
Each comment in the starter marks where a print() or the if/else goes. Fill them in from top to bottom.
Patterns from earlier lessons: print("Welcome, " + name) for the welcome, and if answer == "yes": then else: for the two endings.

errorHints.text: The player's name is stored in hero, and the path in path. Use those exact names.
Lines inside if and else start with four spaces.
Your very first line must be a print() with a scene, before the line that asks for a name.
Keep both input() lines from the starter: the name first, then the path.

similarExample.code:
print("The train doors open.")
rider = input("Ticket name? ")
print("All aboard, " + rider)
similarExample.note: A scene, a question and a welcome. Your adventure adds the path question and two different endings.

otherWays.code:
print("A storm rolls in.")
hero = input("Your name? ")
print(f"Welcome aboard, {hero}!")
path = input("Left or right? ")
if path == "left":
    print("You ride the lightning.")
else:
    print("You shelter in a lighthouse.")
otherWays.note: An f-string for the welcome.

py.u02.title: Count the treasure
py.u02.description: Give your adventure a score, and share out a chest of coins.
py.u02.learn: Numbers in Python have no quotes around them. + adds, - takes away, * multiplies and / divides. print(3 + 4) shows 7, and a variable can hold a number, like score = 10.
py.u02.detail: Two more operators help when you share things out. // divides and keeps only the whole part: 17 // 5 is 3. % gives what is left over: 17 % 5 is 2. As in maths class, Python works out * and / before + and -. Use parentheses to choose a different order.
py.u02.example:
# Work out the hero's score
gems = 4
coins = 13
score = gems * 10 + coins
print(score)
# Share the coins between 5 friends
print(coins // 5)
print(coins % 5)
py.u02.exampleNote: Python works out gems * 10 first, so the score is 40 + 13. Then // gives each friend's whole coins, and % gives the coins left over.
py.u02.question: If coins were 14 instead of 13, what would print(coins % 5) show?
py.u02.why: Five friends take 2 coins each, which uses 10 of the 14. % shows what is left over, so it prints 4. 14 // 5 would show 2, and 14 / 5 would show 2.8.
py.u02.guided: Give gems and coins new values. Before you run, predict all three lines, then run and compare. Try a number of coins that shares out exactly between 5, like 15: what does % show then?
py.u02.starter:
# These two lines ask for whole numbers (lesson 3 explains how)
coins = int(input("How many coins? "))
friends = int(input("How many friends? "))
# Print each friend's whole share, then the coins left over
py.u02.challenge: The party opens a chest of coins to share. The starter asks for the number of coins and the number of friends. Print two lines: how many whole coins each friend gets, then how many coins are left over. Print just the two numbers. The check runs your program with several chests, including some you can't see.
hints: You need two results from the same two numbers: the whole coins each friend gets, and the coins left over.
Look at the comment line. One operator divides and keeps only the whole part; another gives what is left over. Each result goes in its own print().
A pattern with other names: print(cookies // children) shows each child's whole cookies. For the leftover line, use the operator that gives what is left over.

errorHints.text: Use the names the starter made, coins and friends, spelled exactly the same in your print() lines.
Print each number on its own, like print(coins). Joining a number to text with + needs str(), and this check wants only the numbers.
Compare your first line with 3. A decimal point, like 3.4, means / was used: // keeps only the whole coins. Words on the line? Print just the number.
With 3 coins and 5 friends, nobody gets a whole coin, so the first line is 0 and all 3 coins are left over. A division that rounds up would give 1 instead.
Your program needs to work for any chest. Use coins and friends in your calculations, not numbers typed into the code.

similarExample.code:
start = 9
later = start + 14
print(later % 12)
similarExample.note: 14 hours after 9 o'clock, a 12-hour clock shows 11: % keeps what is left after taking away whole groups of 12. Your challenge makes whole groups too, one share for each friend.

otherWays.code:
coins = int(input("How many coins? "))
friends = int(input("How many friends? "))
share, left = divmod(coins, friends)
print(share)
print(left)
otherWays.note: divmod() works out the whole share and the leftover in one step.

otherWays.code:
coins = int(input("How many coins? "))
friends = int(input("How many friends? "))
share = coins // friends
print(share)
print(coins - share * friends)
otherWays.note: The leftover is what remains after every friend takes their share.

py.u02.title: Average the scores
py.u02.description: Find the average of two riddle scores, decimals and all.
py.u02.learn: Python has two kinds of numbers. An int is a whole number, like 7 or -3. A float has a decimal point, like 2.5 or 7.0. Dividing with / always gives a float, even when the answer is whole: 6 / 3 is 2.0.
py.u02.detail: When a calculation mixes an int and a float, the answer is a float: 2 + 0.5 is 2.5. int() cuts off the decimal part without rounding, so int(3.9) is 3 and int(-2.5) is -2. A few decimals print oddly, like 0.1 + 0.2 showing 0.30000000000000004. That comes from how computers store decimals, not from a mistake in your code.
py.u02.example:
# How long the walk to the market takes
distance = 9
speed = 2
hours = distance / speed
print(hours)
# The whole hours, with the decimal part cut off
print(int(hours))
# / gives a float even when the answer is whole
print(8 / 2)
py.u02.exampleNote: hours holds the float 4.5. int() cuts off the .5 and gives the int 4. The last line shows 4.0, not 4, because / always gives a float.
py.u02.question: What would print(int(7.9)) display?
py.u02.why: int() cuts off everything after the decimal point; it does not round up. So int(7.9) is 7, even though 7.9 is close to 8.
py.u02.guided: Change distance to 10. Before you run, predict the first line: will it still have a decimal point? Then change the last line to print(8 // 2), predict again, and compare the two answers.

second = int(input("Second score? "))

Look at the order Python works in: it divides before it adds. Check that your whole total gets divided, not only the second score.
With other names: total = low + high adds first, and then total / 2 halves it. For your second line, think about which function cuts off the decimal part.

Print each number on its own, like print(total). Joining a number to text with + needs str(), and this check wants only the numbers.
The average of 7 and 8 is 7.5. If your first line says 11.0, Python divided only the second score: put the addition inside parentheses.
With -3 and 2, the average is -0.5. int() cuts off the decimal part, so the second line is 0. The // operator rounds down instead, which gives -1 for negative numbers.

py.u02.title: Score the riddle
py.u02.description: Turn the player's replies into numbers, and keep score when a riddle is solved or missed.
py.u02.learn: input() always gives back text, even when the player types digits. So "5" + "5" joins into "55" instead of adding up to 10. int(...) turns text like "12" into the whole number 12, and float(...) turns "2.5" into the decimal 2.5.
py.u02.detail: Wrap the reply in int(), like points = int(input("Points? ")). If the reply is not a whole number, such as ten or an empty reply, int() stops with a ValueError. When a reply might be empty, compare it with "" before you convert it, as the example on the next card does.
py.u02.example:
# Ask for the gold in your pocket, as a whole number
gold = int(input("Gold in your pocket? "))
# Ask for the bridge toll; an empty reply means no toll
toll = input("Toll? ")
if toll == "":
    toll = "0"
# Turn the toll into a number, then pay it
print(gold - int(toll))
py.u02.exampleNote: With 20 and 5 as replies, it prints 15. An empty toll becomes the text "0" first, so int() has a digit to read. Without int(), Python could not take text away from a number.
py.u02.question: If the player types ten in letters for the gold, what happens?
py.u02.why: int() only understands digits, like "10". The letters ten are not a whole number, so Python stops with a ValueError on line 2. You can try it on the next card.
py.u02.guided: Run the example with 20 and 5. Then predict, and run, each of these: an empty toll, and the letters ten as the gold. Last, delete int( and its ) from the gold line, run it, and read the explanation. Reset code puts the example back.
py.u02.starter:
# Ask for the score and turn the reply into a whole number
# Ask for the riddle's points; an empty reply means 0
# Print the score if solved, then the score if missed
py.u02.challenge: The riddle keeper says how many points a riddle is worth. Ask for the hero's score, then for the riddle's points, and turn both replies into whole numbers yourself. Print two lines: the score if the riddle is solved (the points are added), then the score if it is missed (the points are taken away). An empty points reply means a practice riddle worth 0. Print just the two numbers.
hints: Three steps: get the score as a number, get the points as a number (or 0 when the reply is empty), then print the two results.
Look at the second comment. Keep the points reply as text until you have checked whether it is "", and only then turn it into a number.
A pattern with other names: reply = input("Coins? "), then if reply == "": with an indented line that gives reply the text "0", then coins = int(reply).
inputs: Toll (a number, or leave it empty)

errorHints.text: One test leaves the points reply empty, and int() can't turn empty text into a number. Check whether the reply is "" before you call int().
input() gives text. Text can't be taken away from a number, and + joins text instead of adding. Wrap each reply in int(...) before you calculate.
Give each name a value before you use it, spelled the same each time. Each input() reply needs a name of its own.
This challenge gives your program two replies: the score, then the points. Use exactly two input() calls.

Missing a riddle can take the score below zero: 5 - 8 is -3. Print the result as it is; a negative score is fine here.
With an empty points reply, the riddle is worth 0, so both lines show the score unchanged.
Calculate from the replies, not from numbers typed into the code, so your program works for every score.
Every reply counts, even a score of zero. Calculate from the replies rather than checking for particular numbers.

py.u02.title: Too high or too low?
py.u02.description: Compare the player's guess with the riddle keeper's secret number.
py.u02.learn: A comparison asks Python a yes-or-no question about two values. 7 > 5 is True, and 7 < 5 is False. True and False are values too, so print(7 > 5) shows True.
py.u02.detail: There are six comparisons: < (less than), > (greater than), <= (less than or equal to), >= (greater than or equal to), == (equal to) and != (not equal to). Two equals signs compare; one equals sign stores a value. 5 <= 5 is True, but 5 < 5 is False.
py.u02.example:
# The lantern needs at least 3 drops of oil
oil = 5
print(oil >= 3)
# Is the tank completely full at 10?
print(oil == 10)
# Is it empty?
print(oil < 1)
py.u02.exampleNote: oil is 5, so oil >= 3 is True. It is not 10, and it is not less than 1, so the other two lines show False.
py.u02.question: If oil were 3, what would print(oil >= 3) show?
py.u02.why: >= means greater than or equal to. 3 is equal to 3, so the answer is True. print(oil > 3) would show False.
py.u02.guided: Set oil to 3, then to 0. Before each run, predict all three lines, then run and compare. Then change >= to > and see which line changes.
py.u02.starter:
# These two lines ask for the secret number and the guess
secret = int(input("Secret number? "))
guess = int(input("Your guess? "))
# Print True or False: too high, then too low, then exactly right
py.u02.challenge: The riddle keeper has a secret number, and the player makes a guess. The starter asks for both. Print three lines, each True or False: is the guess too high, is it too low, and is it exactly right? Print just the three answers. The check tries several guesses, including some you can't see.
hints: Each line is one comparison between guess and secret. print() of a comparison shows True or False.
Look at the comment. Too high means the guess is bigger than the secret, too low means it is smaller, and right means they are equal. Comparing for equal uses two equals signs.
A pattern with other names: print(height > limit) shows True when height is over the limit. Your three lines compare guess with secret in three different ways.

errorHints.text: Use the names from the starter, secret and guess, spelled exactly the same.
Inside print(), compare with == (two equals signs). A single = inside print() makes Python stop with a TypeError.
Each comparison sign is written together with no space inside it: >=, <=, == and !=. Check the line Python points to.
With a secret of 7 and a guess of 9, the guess is too high, so the lines are True, False, False. Check the order of your three lines.
When the guess equals the secret, it is neither too high nor too low: False, False, True. If your first line says True, you may have used >= where > belongs.
Your comparisons need to work for every number, including ones below zero. Compare guess with secret instead of checking for particular numbers.
Compare guess with secret, not with numbers typed into the code, so your program works for every secret.

similarExample.code:
speed = 45
limit = 50
print(speed > limit)
print(speed != limit)
similarExample.note: A speed of 45 is not over the limit of 50, so the first line is False, and the two are not equal, so the second line is True. Your challenge compares a guess with a secret number in three ways.

otherWays.code:
secret = int(input("Secret number? "))
guess = int(input("Your guess? "))
print(secret < guess)
print(secret > guess)
print(secret == guess)
otherWays.note: A comparison can face the other way: secret < guess means the same as guess > secret.

otherWays.code:

guess = int(input("Your guess? "))

too_low = guess < secret
print(too_high)
print(too_low)
print(not too_high and not too_low)

py.u02.title: Close enough?
py.u02.description: Decide whether a guess is close or out of range by joining comparisons together.
py.u02.learn: and, or and not combine True and False. A and B is True only when both are True. A or B is True when at least one of them is True. not flips True to False, and False to True.
py.u02.detail: Each side of and or or is a whole comparison: write x > 0 and x < 10, not x > 0 and < 10. Python works out the comparisons first, then not, then and, then or. Use parentheses when you want to be sure of the order.
py.u02.example:
# The bridge is safe for 2 to 6 travellers
travellers = 7
print(travellers >= 2 and travellers <= 6)
# Too few or too many?
print(travellers < 2 or travellers > 6)
# Flip the first answer with not
print(not (travellers >= 2 and travellers <= 6))
py.u02.exampleNote: 7 is at least 2 but more than 6, so the and line is False. The or line needs only one side to be True, and 7 > 6 is. not flips the first answer from False to True.
py.u02.question: If travellers were 2, what would the first print() show?
py.u02.why: 2 >= 2 is True and 2 <= 6 is True. With and, both sides are True, so the whole line is True.
py.u02.guided: Try travellers = 2, then 6, then 0, and predict the three lines before each run. Then change and to or in the first print(). Find a number of travellers where the answer changes, and explain why.
py.u02.starter:
# Ask for the secret number, then the guess, as whole numbers
# Print True or False: close, out of range, not close
py.u02.challenge: The riddle keeper's secret number is always from 1 to 100. Ask for the secret and the guess, as whole numbers. Print three lines, each True or False: is the guess close (no more than 2 away from the secret, on either side); is the guess out of range (below 1 or above 100); and is the guess not close? Print just the three answers.
hints: Three lines, three joined questions. Close needs two comparisons joined with and. Out of range needs two joined with or. The last line flips the first one with not.
Close means the guess is at least secret - 2 and at most secret + 2. Out of range means below 1 or above 100. Check whether each limit should use < or <=.
A pattern with other names: print(depth >= low and depth <= high) checks that depth sits between two limits. Putting not ( ) around a question flips its answer.

errorHints.text: Each side of and and or needs a whole comparison, like guess >= 1 and guess <= 100. Writing guess >= 1 and <= 100 makes Python stop.
Give secret and guess their values from input() before you compare them, and spell them the same each time.
A guess of 53 is 3 away from 50, so it is not close. If your first line says True, check whether you joined the two limits with or: or is True when either side is, and here one side always is.
52 is exactly 2 away from 50, which still counts as close. Check that your limits use <= and >=, so the edge is included.
0 is below 1, so it is out of range: True. Out of range needs or, because a guess can't be below 1 and above 100 at the same time.
Check both ends of the range: a guess equal to the highest or lowest allowed answer is still in range.
A guess equal to the lowest allowed answer is still in range, and a guess 1 away from the secret is close. Check each < against <=.

temperature = 18
print(temperature >= 15 and temperature <= 25)
print(not temperature > 30)
similarExample.note: 18 is between 15 and 25, so the first line is True, and 18 is not over 30, so the second line is True too. Your challenge checks a guess against limits that come from the secret number.

print(close)
print(guess < 1 or guess > 100)
print(not close)
otherWays.note: Python lets you chain two comparisons, which reads like maths: low <= x <= high.

py.u02.title: The riddle keeper's verdict
py.u02.description: Give points for a guess by how close it is, choosing exactly one branch.
py.u02.learn: if and else choose between two paths. elif, short for "else if", adds more. Python checks each condition from the top and runs only the first block whose condition is True. It skips the rest.
py.u02.detail: Order matters when conditions overlap. A guess that is exactly right is also close, so check for exactly right first. else catches everything the conditions above it did not. Each elif line ends with a colon, and its block is indented by four spaces.
py.u02.exampleNote: 12 >= 25 is False, so Python moves on. 12 >= 10 is True, so it prints wool cloak and skips else. With 30, only light cloak prints, even though 30 >= 10 is True as well.
py.u02.question: If temperature were 30, what would the program print?
py.u02.why: Python runs only the first block whose condition is True. 30 >= 25 is True, so light cloak prints, and the elif and else are skipped.
py.u02.guided: Predict the cloak for 25, 10 and 9, then run each one. Next, change elif to if, run with 30 and compare: why do two lines print now? Reset code puts the example back.
py.u02.starter:
# Ask for the secret number and the guess

py.u02.challenge: The riddle keeper gives points for a guess: 10 if it is exactly right, 5 if it is close (no more than 2 away), 1 if it is no more than 10 away, and 0 otherwise. Ask for the secret number and the guess, then print the points. Print just the number.

Look at the order of your checks. A guess that is exactly right is also close, so ask about exactly right first, then close, then within 10, and let else give 0.

errorHints.text: if, elif and else lines end with a colon, and comparing for equal uses ==. An elif must come straight after an if block or another elif block.
The line under each if, elif and else starts with four spaces. Press Tab at the start of the line to add them.
Ask for both numbers with input() and give them names before your if line, spelled the same each time.
An exactly right guess scores 10, printed once. Separate if statements can all run; in an if and elif chain only the first match does. Put the exact check first.
42 is 2 away from 40, so it scores 5. If you printed 1, check the order of your conditions. If you printed two numbers, use elif so only one branch runs.
50 is exactly 10 away from 40, which still scores 1. Check that this limit uses <= or >=, so the edge counts.
51 is 11 away, more than 10, so it scores 0. else is the place for everything the other branches did not catch.
Guesses below the secret count too: close and within 10 mean on either side. Use and to check both limits, or work out how far away the guess is.
A guess far below the secret scores 0. Check that your within-10 test has a lower limit as well as an upper one.
Compare guess with secret, not with numbers typed into the code, so your program works for every secret.

similarExample.note: A ticket price by age: under 5 is free, under 13 costs 4, and everyone else pays 8. A 9 year old matches only the second condition, so only 4 prints. Your challenge has four outcomes and compares two numbers.

Separate if statements work here because each later check replaces the points with a bigger score, and only one number is printed at the end.

py.u03.title: Keep guessing
py.u03.description: Let the player keep guessing the secret number until they get it right.
py.u03.learn: A while loop repeats a block of code for as long as its condition is True. Python checks the condition, runs the indented block, then checks again. When the condition becomes False, the loop ends and the program carries on below it.
py.u03.detail: Something inside the loop must change, or the condition stays True forever. To keep asking the player, call input() once before the loop and again at the end of the block. If the condition is False the very first time, the block never runs at all.
py.u03.example:
# Keep asking until the password is moon
word = input("Password? ")
while word != "moon":
    print("The door stays shut.")
    word = input("Password? ")
print("The door opens.")
py.u03.exampleOutput:
The door stays shut.
The door stays shut.
The door opens.
py.u03.exampleNote: The condition is checked before each repeat. star and sun are not moon, so the block runs twice. When word becomes moon, the condition is False, the loop ends, and the last line runs.
py.u03.question: If the first reply were moon, what would the program print?
options: The door stays shut. once, then The door opens.
py.u03.why: word != "moon" is False straight away, so the block never runs. Python goes on to the last line and prints The door opens.
py.u03.guided: Run it, then change the replies so that moon comes first, then last. Predict how many times The door stays shut. appears before each run. Then try three wrong replies and read what happens when the replies run out.
py.u03.starter:
# These two lines ask for the secret number and the first guess
secret = int(input("Secret number? "))
guess = int(input("Your guess? "))
# While the guess is wrong: print whether it is too high, then ask again
py.u03.challenge: The riddle keeper lets the player keep guessing. The starter asks for the secret number and the first guess. While the guess is wrong, print True if it is too high or False if it is too low, then ask for another guess. When the guess is right, the loop ends. Print just the True and False lines. The check tries several runs of guesses, including some you can't see.
hints: You need a loop that repeats while the guess is not the secret. Inside it, two things happen: a print() and a new guess.
Look at the comment. The loop's condition compares guess with secret using !=. The last line inside the loop asks for the next guess, the same way the starter asked for the first one.
A pattern from the worked example: while word != "moon": with an indented print(), then an indented line that asks again. Your loop compares numbers instead of words.

errorHints.text: Your loop asked for another guess after the last reply. Check that it stops as soon as the guess is right: that is when its condition should become False.
Use the names from the starter, secret and guess, and spell them the same inside the loop.
The lines inside the loop start with four spaces, so Python knows they belong to it.
Each new guess needs int(...) too, like the first one. Python can't compare text with a number using >.
With a secret of 7 and guesses of 9, 3 and 7, the lines are True, then False. If only True printed, your program checked once with if; a while loop checks again after every guess.
When the first guess is right, the loop never runs and nothing is printed. If your program printed a line, check that the print() is inside the loop.
Three low guesses print three False lines. Make sure your loop keeps going for as long as the guess is wrong, however many guesses that takes.
Guesses below zero compare the same way. Compare guess with secret, not with particular numbers.
Your loop needs to keep going for as many wrong guesses as the player makes, not for a fixed number of them.

print(steps)

while True repeats until break leaves the loop, so input() is written only once. The next lesson looks at how loops end.

py.u03.title: Three tries
py.u03.description: Give the player three tries, and make sure the loop always ends.
py.u03.learnTitle: Every loop needs a way out
py.u03.learn: A loop ends only when its condition becomes False. Something inside the loop has to move it there: a counter that goes up or down, or a new reply. If nothing changes, the loop runs forever.
py.u03.detail: A counter often decides how many times a loop runs. Starting it at 0 or at 1, and choosing < or <=, changes the count by one. To stop for either of two reasons, join the conditions with and: keep going while the guess is wrong and tries are left. Here, a program that never ends is stopped for you after a few seconds.
py.u03.example:
# Count down to the gate opening
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1
print("open")
py.u03.exampleNote: count goes 3, 2, 1. After 1 is printed it becomes 0, so count > 0 is False and the loop ends. The last line runs once, after the loop.
py.u03.question: If the line count = count - 1 were deleted, what would happen?
options: It would still print 3, 2, 1 and open
It would print 3 again and again and never finish
Python would stop with an error at once
py.u03.why: count would stay 3, so count > 0 would always be True and the loop would never end. Because it prints each time, the academy stops it as soon as the output gets too long. You can try it on the next card.
py.u03.guided: Predict, then run: change count = 3 to count = 5. Next, delete the line count = count - 1 and run it; the academy stops the program and explains why. Put the line back with Reset code. Last, change > to >= and count how many numbers print.
py.u03.starter:
# Ask for the secret number and the first guess
# Keep asking while the guess is wrong and tries are left
# Then print the number of guesses, and whether the last one was right
py.u03.challenge: The riddle keeper allows three tries. Ask for the secret number, then ask for guesses until the guess is right or three guesses have been made. After the loop, print two lines: how many guesses were made, then True if the last guess was right or False if it was not. Print just the two answers.
hints: Count the guesses as you go. The loop needs two reasons to keep going, joined with and: the guess is wrong, and fewer than three guesses have been made.
Check your counter: after the first guess it should be 1. Each time the loop asks again, add 1. With three tries, the loop can ask at most two more times.
A pattern with other names: while answer != key and turns < 5: with indented lines that ask again and add 1 to turns.

errorHints.text: Your loop asked for another guess after the last reply. It should stop after three guesses, even when none of them is right: check the counter in the loop's condition.
Give every name a value before the loop uses it, including the counter, and spell it the same each time.
Here the third guess is right, so the lines are 3 and True. If your program stopped after two guesses, check where your counter starts and whether you used < or <=.
Three wrong guesses use up the tries, so the second line is False. Print whether the last guess equals the secret, rather than True every time.
When the first guess is right, the loop never runs: one guess, and True. Check that your counter is 1 after the first guess.
Only the first three guesses count, so the lines are 3 and False, even though a fourth reply would be right. If your program printed 4 and True, the loop needs a limit on tries.
Count every guess, including the first one, so the number printed is right whichever try solves the riddle.
A secret below zero works the same way. Compare the guess with the secret instead of checking for particular numbers.

    guess = int(input("Your guess? "))

py.u03.title: Step by step
py.u03.description: Count the steps of a staircase with a for loop and range(), two at a time.
py.u03.learn: A for loop runs its block once for each value it is given. range(1, 4) gives 1, 2 and 3: it starts at the first number and stops before the second. So for n in range(1, 4): with print(n) inside prints 1, 2 and 3.
py.u03.detail: range(4) on its own gives 0, 1, 2 and 3. A third number sets the step: range(2, 9, 2) gives 2, 4, 6 and 8, and a step of -1 counts down. To include a number at the end, make the stop one bigger. A for loop moves its own variable on each time, so it always ends.
py.u03.exampleNote: range(1, 6) stops before 6, so the planks are 1 to 5. A step of -1 counts down: range(3, 0, -1) gives 3, 2 and 1, and stops before 0.
py.u03.question: What would for n in range(2, 7, 2): with print(n) inside print?
py.u03.why: It starts at 2 and adds 2 each time: 2, 4, 6. The next number would be 8, but range stops before 7, so 8 is never reached.
py.u03.guided: Predict, then run: change range(1, 6) to range(1, 11). Then make the countdown start at 10. Last, change the countdown's step to -2 and predict the numbers before you run.
py.u03.starter: # Ask for the top step, then print every step the hero lands on
py.u03.challenge: The hero climbs the riddle keeper's staircase two steps at a time, starting on step 2. Ask for the number of the top step, then print every step the hero lands on, up to and including the top step if they land on it. Print just the step numbers, one per line.
hints: The hero lands on 2, 4, 6 and so on. A for loop over a range() with a step of 2 gives exactly those numbers.
range() stops before its second number. For a top step of 8, the stop has to be bigger than 8, or step 8 is missed.
A pattern with other names: for seat in range(1, rows + 1, 3): gives 1, 4, 7 and so on, up to rows. Your loop starts at a different number and steps by 2.

errorHints.text: range() needs whole numbers. Turn the reply into a number with int(...) before you use it.
Use the same name for the top step everywhere, and give it a value with input() before the loop.
The line inside the for loop starts with four spaces.
With a top step of 8, the hero lands on 2, 4, 6 and 8. If 8 is missing, the stop of your range() is 8: make it one bigger.
With a top step of 7, the hero lands on 2, 4 and 6, never on 8, which is above the top. Check the stop of your range().
With a top step of 1, the hero never lands on a step, so nothing is printed. A range() that starts above its stop gives no numbers at all.
Use the reply in your range(), not numbers typed into the code, so it works for every staircase.
Check odd top steps as well as even ones: the last step printed is the biggest even number that is not above the top.

similarExample.code:
for floor in range(10, 0, -3):
    print(floor)
similarExample.note: Starting at floor 10 and going down 3 at a time gives 10, 7, 4 and 1. The stop, 0, is never printed. Your challenge counts up by 2 and has to reach the top step.

otherWays.code:
top = int(input("Top step? "))
step = 2
while step <= top:
    print(step)
    step = step + 2
otherWays.note: The same steps with a while loop. for and range() do the counting for you, so they are the tidy way, but this works too.
Go through every step and print only the even ones: step % 2 == 0 means no remainder after dividing by 2.

py.u03.title: Keep the score
py.u03.description: Add up the points from every round of the riddle keeper's game, count the empty rounds, and find the average.
py.u03.learnTitle: Build up an answer, one turn at a time
py.u03.learn: A running total starts at 0 before the loop. Inside the loop, total = total + coins adds this turn's number to what is already there. When the loop ends, total holds the sum of them all.
py.u03.detail: A counter works the same way, but adds 1 each time something happens, often inside an if. The start line goes above the loop, so it runs once: inside the loop it would wipe the total every turn. For an average, divide the total by how many numbers there were, after the loop.
py.u03.example:
# Three chests: add up the coins, then find the average
chests = 3
total = 0
for chest in range(chests):
    coins = int(input("Coins in this chest? "))
    total = total + coins
print(total)
print(total / chests)
py.u03.exampleNote: total starts at 0 and grows: 4, then 4 again, then 12. The two print lines are below the loop, not indented, so they run once, after the last chest. Dividing with / always gives a float, so the average shows as 4.0.
py.u03.question: Suppose total = 0 moves inside the loop, as the first line of its block. With the same replies, what would print(total) show?
py.u03.why: total goes back to 0 at the start of every turn, so each chest forgets the ones before it. Only the last chest's 8 is left when the loop ends.
py.u03.guided: Predict, then run: move total = 0 inside the loop, as the first line of its block, and check your prediction. Put it back above the loop. Then add a counter for empty chests: start it above the loop, add 1 inside an if, and print it at the end.
py.u03.starter: # Ask for the rounds, then the points from each round
py.u03.challenge: The riddle keeper's game now has rounds. Ask how many rounds were played (always at least 1), then ask for the points from each round. Print three lines: the total points, how many rounds scored 0, and the average points per round, using /. Print just the numbers.
hints: You need two things that build up as the loop runs, and both start at 0 above the loop: one for the points, and one for the rounds that scored 0.
A for loop over range() runs once per round. Ask for that round's points inside it. The three print lines go after the loop, with no indent.
A pattern with other names: start with distance = 0, and inside the loop use distance = distance + miles. Your loop also needs a counter, and an if to decide when it goes up.

errorHints.text: A reply from input() is text. Turn it into a number with int(...) before you add it up or use it in range().
Give each name a value before the loop uses it, and spell it the same way every time.
The lines that repeat start with four spaces. A line inside an if inside the loop starts with eight.
Your loop asked for more points than there were rounds. range(rounds) already runs exactly once per round.
The average divides by the number of rounds played, and that is always at least 1. Check which number comes after the /.
With one round of 10 points, the lines are 10, 0 and 10.0. A total or a counter that starts above 0 is already wrong here, and // gives 10 where / gives 10.0.
With rounds of 10, 0 and 5, the lines are 15, 1 and 5.0. If your total says 5, it goes back to 0 on every turn: its start line belongs above the loop.
With two rounds of 0, the lines are 0, 2 and 0.0. Every round that scores 0 counts, even when nothing has been scored yet.
Check a longer game: use the number of rounds in range() and in the average, and / rather than //, which throws away the part after the point.
Check a game with more than one empty round: the counter goes up every time a round scores 0.

similarExample.code:
gold = 1
for day in range(3):
    gold = gold * 2
print(gold)
similarExample.note: Another answer that builds up: the gold doubles each day, giving 8 after three days. It starts at 1, because doubling 0 would stay 0. Your challenge adds up every round and counts the empty ones instead.

otherWays.code:
rounds = int(input("Rounds? "))
total = 0
empty = 0
count = 0
while count < rounds:
    points = int(input("Points? "))
    total = total + points
    if points == 0:
        empty = empty + 1
    count = count + 1
print(total)
print(empty)
print(total / rounds)
otherWays.note: The same totals with a while loop, which needs its own count of the rounds so far. for and range() do that counting for you.

otherWays.code:
rounds = int(input("Rounds? "))
total = 0
scored = 0
for game in range(rounds):
    points = int(input("Points? "))
    total += points
    if points > 0:
        scored += 1
print(total)
print(rounds - scored)
print(total / rounds)
otherWays.note: Count the rounds that scored instead, and take them away from all the rounds. += is a short way to write total = total + points.

py.u03.title: Rooms on the map
py.u03.concept: Loops · a loop inside a loop
py.u03.description: Walk the riddle keeper's map row by row, count the coins in each room, and add them all up.
py.u03.learnTitle: Put a loop inside a loop
py.u03.learn: A loop's block can hold another loop. The inner loop runs all the way through, every time the outer loop goes round once. So an outer loop of 2 turns and an inner loop of 3 turns runs the inner block 6 times.
py.u03.detail: The outer loop's line starts at the left, the inner loop's line has four spaces, and the inner block has eight. for and range() start the inner loop again by themselves. With while, the inner counter has to be set back to its start inside the outer loop, or the inner loop only runs the first time.
py.u03.exampleNote: row starts at 1, and seat runs through 1, 2 and 3. Then row becomes 2, and seat starts again from 1. Multiplying by 10 is just a way to show both numbers at once: 23 is row 2, seat 3.
py.u03.question: If the two for lines swapped places, so that seat is the outer loop and row the inner one, what would the first three lines print?
py.u03.why: The inner loop finishes first. seat stays at 1 while row runs through 1 and 2, giving 11 and 21. Then seat becomes 2 and row starts again, giving 12.
py.u03.guided: Predict, then run: swap the two for lines, with row and seat keeping their ranges. Put them back. Then change range(1, 3) to range(1, 4) and predict how many lines print before you run.
py.u03.starter: # Ask for the rows and the columns, then walk the map
py.u03.challenge: The riddle keeper's map is a grid of rooms. Rows and columns are counted from 1, and a room holds its row number times its column number in coins, so row 2, column 3 holds 6. Ask for the number of rows, then the number of columns. Going through the rows in order, and left to right along each row, print the coins in every room, one per line. On the last line, print the total coins. Print just the numbers.
hints: One for loop goes through the rows. Inside its block, another for loop goes through the columns of that row.
Rows and columns count from 1, and range() stops before its second number. The total starts at 0 above both loops, and prints below both of them.
A pattern with other names: for shelf in range(1, shelves + 1): holds for book in range(1, books + 1): one step further in. The rooms need your own names, your own sum, and a total.

errorHints.text: range() needs whole numbers. Turn each reply into a number with int(...) before you use it.
Use one name for the rows and one for the columns, and give each a value with input() before the loops.
Each loop's block goes four spaces further in than its for line: four for the inner for line, and eight for the lines inside it.
This program needs only two replies, the rows and the columns. Ask for them once, above the loops.

With 2 rows of 3 columns, the coins go 1, 2, 3, then 2, 4, 6, and the total is 18. If you see 1, 2, 2, 4, 3, 6, the two loops are the wrong way round. If only the first row printed, the inner counter did not start again.
With 3 rows of 2 columns, the coins go 1, 2, then 2, 4, then 3, 6. Use the replies in your range() calls, not numbers typed into the code.
A map of one room holds 1 coin, so the lines are 1 and then the total, 1. The total line is always printed.
Check a map with more rows than the examples: the outer range() has to follow the rows reply.
Check a map with more columns than the examples: the inner range() has to follow the columns reply.

similarExample.note: A clock that strikes every half hour shows 100, 130, 200 and 230: for each hour, the minutes start again from 0. Your challenge goes through rows and columns, counts from 1, and adds everything up.

otherWays.code:
rows = int(input("Rows? "))
columns = int(input("Columns? "))
total = 0
row = 1
while row <= rows:
    column = 1
    while column <= columns:
        print(row * column)
        total = total + row * column
        column = column + 1
    row = row + 1
print(total)
otherWays.note: The same walk with while loops. Look at column = 1: it sits inside the outer loop, so each row starts again from the first column. for and range() do that for you.

otherWays.code:
rows = int(input("Rows? "))
columns = int(input("Columns? "))
total = 0
for room in range(rows * columns):
    row = room // columns + 1
    column = room % columns + 1
    print(row * column)
    total = total + row * column
print(total)
otherWays.note: One loop over every room, working out its row and column with // and %. It is correct and clever, but two loops say what you mean more plainly.

py.u04.title: Pack the bag
py.u04.description: Pack the hero's bag one item at a time, count what is in it, and check whether something was packed.
py.u04.learnTitle: Keep many things under one name
py.u04.learn: A list holds several values in order, inside square brackets: pack = ["rope", "map"]. pack.append("lamp") adds one more to the end, and len(pack) says how many there are.
py.u04.detail: item in pack is True when the item is somewhere in the list, and False when it is not. append() changes the list itself and gives back nothing, so it goes on a line of its own: pack.append("lamp"). An empty list, [], has a length of 0.
py.u04.example:
# Pack for the journey
pack = ["rope", "map"]
pack.append("lantern")
print(len(pack))
print("map" in pack)
print("sword" in pack)
print(pack)
py.u04.exampleNote: append() put lantern at the end, so the pack holds three things. in looks through the whole list for an exact match. print(pack) shows the list the way Python writes one, with brackets and quotes.
py.u04.question: Suppose the third line were pack = pack.append("lantern"), and the only print were print(pack). What would it show?
py.u04.why: append() changes the list and gives back None. Storing that None in pack replaces the whole list with it.
py.u04.guided: Predict, then run: add one more item with append() and check that len() goes up by one. Then make the first line pack = [] and see what len(pack) and print(pack) show for a pack that starts empty.
py.u04.starter: # Ask how many items, then pack them one at a time
py.u04.challenge: Pack the hero's bag. Ask how many items to pack (it can be 0), then ask for each item and add it to a list. Then ask for one more item to look for. Print three lines: how many items are in the pack, True or False for whether the item you looked for is in it, and the pack itself, with print(). Print just those three lines.
hints: You need a list that starts empty, above the loop, and grows by one item each time round the loop.
A for loop over range() asks once per item. After the loop, one more input() gives the item to look for, and in tells you whether it is there.
The same pattern with other names: shelf = [] goes before the loop, and shelf.append(book) goes inside it. len(shelf) counts the books.

errorHints.text: range() needs a number. Turn the first reply into one with int(...) before the loop.
append() changes the list and gives back None. Write the append on its own line, without storing what it gives back.
Your program asked for one more reply than it gets. range() with the number of items runs exactly once per item, and the item to look for comes after the loop.
Make the list before the loop uses it, and spell its name the same way every time.
With three items packed and map looked for, the lines are 3, True and the whole list. If your count says 1, the list starts again inside the loop: make it once, above the loop.
When the item looked for was never packed, the answer is False. Check that you look through the whole pack, not just one item of it.
With 0 items the loop runs no times, the length is 0, and print() shows an empty list as [].
Pack every reply, even one that is already in the pack. A list can hold the same thing twice.
Check a longer pack: the loop should run once for every item, however many there are.

similarExample.code:
songs = []
songs.append("river tune")
songs.append("night song")
print(len(songs))
print("river tune" in songs)
similarExample.note: Another list that grows: two songs added one at a time, then counted and searched. Your challenge reads its items from the player, in a loop.

otherWays.code:
count = int(input("How many items? "))
pack = []
while len(pack) < count:
    pack.append(input("Item? "))
wanted = input("Look for? ")
print(len(pack))
print(pack.count(wanted) > 0)
print(pack)
otherWays.note: The loop can stop when the pack is full, using len(). count() says how many times a value is in the list, so more than 0 means it is there.

otherWays.code:
count = int(input("How many items? "))
pack = []
for n in range(count):
    pack = pack + [input("Item? ")]
wanted = input("Look for? ")
print(len(pack))
print(wanted in pack)
print(pack)
otherWays.note: + joins two lists into a new one, so pack = pack + [item] also grows the pack. append() changes the list you already have, which is quicker for long lists.

py.u04.title: First and last
py.u04.description: Pick supplies out of the quartermaster's list by their position, and slice off the middle.
py.u04.learn: Positions in a list start at 0. In pack = ["rope", "map", "lamp"], pack[0] is "rope" and pack[2] is "lamp". A negative position counts from the end, so pack[-1] is the last item.
py.u04.detail: pack[1] = "key" puts a new value at position 1, replacing what was there. A slice such as pack[0:2] is a new list of the items from position 0 up to, but not including, position 2. Asking for a position past the end, like pack[3] here, stops the program with an IndexError.
py.u04.example:
# Pick tools from the pack by position
pack = ["rope", "map", "lamp", "key"]
print(pack[0])
print(pack[-1])
print(pack[1:3])
pack[0] = "ladder"
print(pack)
py.u04.exampleNote: pack[0] is the first item and pack[-1] the last. The slice 1:3 starts at position 1 and stops before 3, so it holds two items. Assigning to pack[0] replaces rope, and the list keeps its length.
py.u04.question: With the same four items, what does print(pack[len(pack) - 1]) show?
py.u04.why: len(pack) is 4, so len(pack) - 1 is 3, the last position. pack[len(pack)] would be the IndexError: a list of 4 has no position 4.
py.u04.guided: Predict, then run: add print(pack[4]) and read the error. Then change it to show the last item, in two different ways.
py.u04.starter: # Ask for the supplies, then a position
py.u04.challenge: The quartermaster lists the party's supplies. Ask how many supplies there are (always at least 1), then ask for each one, in order. Then ask for a position, counting from 1 the way people do. Print four lines: the first supply, the last supply, the supply at the position asked for, and a list of every supply except the first and the last. Print just those four lines.
hints: Collect the supplies in a list first. Positions start at 0, so the first supply is at 0, and a person who says position 1 means Python position 0.
A negative position counts from the end. A slice gives a list: it starts at its first number and stops just before its second, and either number can be negative.
With other names: name = songs[0] is the first song, name = songs[-1] the last, and the song a person calls number is one position earlier than number.

errorHints.text: A position is past the end of the list. The last item of a list of 4 is at 3, which is also -1, and a person's position 1 is Python's 0.
Positions and range() need whole numbers: turn the number replies into them with int(...).
Your program asked for more replies than it gets. Read the supplies with a loop that runs once per supply, then read the position.
Make the list before the loop uses it, and spell each name the same way every time.
With bread, rope, tent and lamp, and position 2, the lines are bread, lamp, rope and ['rope', 'tent']. If you got tent, the position needs turning into Python's, which starts at 0.
With two supplies there is nothing between the first and the last, so the slice is an empty list, [].
With one supply, it is the first, the last and position 1 all at once.
Check a longer list: the middle slice should keep every supply between the first and the last.
Check position 1: it is the first supply, at Python position 0.

similarExample.code:
days = ["mon", "tue", "wed", "thu", "fri"]
print(days[2])
print(days[-2])
print(days[:2])
similarExample.note: The same positions in a week: the middle day, the day before last, and a slice from the start, because a slice with no first number starts at 0.

supplies = []
for n in range(count):

position = int(input("Position? "))
print(supplies[0])

otherWays.note: len() - 1 is the last position too. -1 is shorter, and works for a list of any length.

supplies = []
for n in range(count):

position = int(input("Position? "))

py.u04.title: Market day
py.u04.description: Go through every treasure in the list: add them up, keep the valuable ones, and find the biggest.
py.u04.learn: for price in prices: runs its block once for each item in the list, in order, with price holding that item. Nothing needs counting: the loop stops after the last item.
py.u04.detail: Inside the loop you can add up, remember the biggest so far, or keep some items: start an empty list and append only the ones an if lets through. Build a new list rather than adding to or removing from the list you are looping over. sum() and max() do two of these jobs for you, but max() of an empty list is an error.
py.u04.example:
# Prices at the market stall
prices = [4, 12, 7, 3]
total = 0
cheap = []
for price in prices:
    total = total + price
    if price < 5:
        cheap.append(price)
print(total)
print(cheap)
print(max(prices))
py.u04.exampleNote: The loop visits 4, 12, 7 and 3. Every price adds to total, and only prices under 5 go into cheap. max() finds the biggest without a loop.
py.u04.question: What would print(cheap) show if the if line said price > 5 instead?
py.u04.why: Only 12 and 7 are more than 5, and they go in in the order the loop meets them.
py.u04.guided: Predict, then run: change the 5 to 10 and check which prices go into cheap. Then add a counter that counts the prices over 5.
py.u04.starter: # Read the treasure values, then the limit
py.u04.challenge: Treasure hunt: ask how many treasures were found (it can be 0), then ask for the value of each one, as a whole number. Then ask for the hero's limit. Print three lines: the total value, a list of the values that are more than the limit, in the order they were found, and the biggest value, or 0 if nothing was found. Print just those three lines.
hints: Keep the values in a list as you read them, because the limit only comes after them.
One loop over the list can do the rest: add each value to a total, keep the ones over the limit in a new list, and remember the biggest so far. All three start before that loop.
With other names: for score in scores: visits each score, and if score > best: followed by best = score keeps the best one.

errorHints.text: max() of an empty list is an error. When nothing was found the biggest is 0: start a biggest-so-far at 0, or check that the list has something in it first.
Turn each reply into a number with int(...) before you add it up or compare it.
Your program asked for more replies than it gets. Read one value per treasure, then the limit.
Give the total, the list and the biggest a value before the loop uses them.
With values 5, 20, 10 and 40 and a limit of 10, the lines are 75, [20, 40] and 40. 10 is not more than 10, so it stays out.
When no value is more than the limit, the list of big ones is empty: [].
With no treasures the total is 0, the list is [], and the biggest is 0.
Check a hunt where every value beats the limit: every one belongs in the list.
Check a hunt where the biggest value is found last: look at every value, to the end.

similarExample.code:
temps = [12, 18, 9, 21]
warm = []
for t in temps:
    if t > 15:
        warm.append(t)
print(warm)
print(len(warm))
similarExample.note: Keeping only some items: the warm days. Your challenge also adds up every value and finds the biggest.

otherWays.note: sum() and max() do the adding and the finding. An empty list counts as False in an if, so max() is only asked when there is something to look at.

count = int(input("Treasures? "))
values = []
total = 0
biggest = 0
for n in range(count):
    value = int(input("Value? "))
    values.append(value)
    total += value
    biggest = max(biggest, value)
limit = int(input("Limit? "))
over = []

print(biggest)
