py.u04.title: Rooms of the keep
py.u04.description: Remember what is in every room of the keep, look a room up by its name, and cope with a room that is not there.
py.u04.learn: A dictionary pairs each key with a value: rooms = {"hall": "lamp", "cellar": "rope"}. rooms["hall"] gives "lamp". Keys must match exactly, so "Hall" is a different key.
py.u04.detail: rooms["tower"] = "key" adds a pair, or replaces the value if that key is already there. rooms["attic"], for a key that is not there, stops with a KeyError; rooms.get("attic", "nothing") gives "nothing" instead. for room, item in rooms.items(): visits each pair, in the order the keys were first added.
py.u04.example:
# What is in each room?
rooms = {"hall": "lamp", "cellar": "rope"}
rooms["tower"] = "key"
rooms["hall"] = "map"
print(rooms["cellar"])
print(rooms.get("attic", "nothing"))
for room, item in rooms.items():
    print(room, item)
py.u04.exampleOutput:
rope
nothing
hall map
cellar rope
tower key
py.u04.exampleNote: hall already had a value, so it changed to map without moving. get() gives its second value for a key that is missing. items() goes through the pairs in the order the keys were first added.
py.u04.question: What would print(rooms["attic"]) do here?
py.u04.why: Square brackets need the key to be there. get() is the gentle way to ask about a key that may be missing.
py.u04.guided: Predict, then run: print len(rooms), add a fourth room, and print it again. Then look up "Hall", with a capital, using get(), and see what comes back.
py.u04.starter: # Read each room and what it holds, then the room to search
py.u04.challenge: Each room of the keep holds one thing. Ask how many rooms there are, then for each room ask for its name and then what it holds. A room named twice is one room, holding the thing given last. Then ask for a room to search. Print three lines: what the searched room holds, or empty if there is no such room; how many rooms there are; and the whole dictionary, with print(). Print just those three lines.
hints: Make an empty dictionary, {}, before the loop. Each time round, read a name and a thing, and pair them, with the name as the key.
Assigning to a key that is already there replaces its value, which is just what a room named twice needs. get() with a second value answers for a room that is not there.
With other names: prices = {} before the loop, then prices[fruit] = cost inside it. prices.get(fruit, 0) gives 0 for a fruit with no price.

errorHints.text: That room is not a key in the dictionary. get() with a second value answers without stopping the program.
range() needs a whole number: use int(...) on the number of rooms.
Your program asked for more replies than it gets. Each room has two replies, its name and then its thing, and the room to search comes after the loop.
Make the dictionary before the loop uses it, and spell its name the same way every time.
With hall, cellar and tower, searching cellar gives rope. Check which reply is the key and which is the value: the name is the key.
A room that is not there gives the word empty, not None and not an error.
A room named twice keeps the thing given last. Assigning to the same key again replaces its value.
Check a keep with no rooms: the count is 0 and print() shows an empty dictionary as {}.
Check names that differ only in capital letters: keys must match exactly, so they are different rooms.

similarExample.code:
ages = {"Ada": 15, "Ben": 14}
ages["Cy"] = 16
ages["Ada"] = 16
print(ages.get("Dee", "unknown"))
print(ages)
similarExample.note: Names and ages instead of rooms and things: a new key adds a pair, an old key gets a new value, and get() answers for a missing one.

otherWays.note: in works on a dictionary too: it checks the keys. Once you know the key is there, square brackets are safe.

otherWays.code:
count = int(input("Rooms? "))
rooms = {}
while count > 0:
    name = input("Room? ")
    thing = input("Holds? ")
    rooms.update({name: thing})
    count -= 1
print(rooms.get(input("Search? "), "empty"))
print(len(rooms))
print(rooms)
otherWays.note: update() adds every pair of another dictionary, replacing values for keys already there. The search reply can go straight into get().

py.u04.title: Rooms already visited
py.u04.description: Keep track of the rooms two explorers have seen, with no repeats, and compare where they have been.
py.u04.learn: A set holds values with no repeats: visited = {"hall", "cellar"}. visited.add("hall") changes nothing, because hall is already in it, and len(visited) counts each value once.
py.u04.detail: An empty set is written set(), because {} is an empty dictionary. A set has no positions and no fixed order, so to print one dependably use sorted(visited), which gives a sorted list. a | b holds everything in either set, a & b only what is in both, and a - b what is in a but not in b.
py.u04.example:
# Where have the two explorers been?
kai = {"hall", "cellar", "tower"}
nova = {"tower", "garden"}
kai.add("hall")
print(len(kai))
print(sorted(kai | nova))
print(sorted(kai & nova))
print("garden" in kai)
py.u04.exampleNote: Adding hall again leaves three rooms. | joins the two sets with no repeats, & keeps the one room both have visited, and sorted() lists them in alphabetical order.
py.u04.question: What would print(len(kai | nova)) show?
py.u04.why: There are five names in the two sets, but tower is in both and is counted once.
py.u04.guided: Predict, then run: add "garden" to kai and print sorted(kai & nova) again. Then try visited = {} followed by visited.add("hall"), and read the error.
py.u04.challenge: Two explorers walk the keep. Ask how many rooms the first explorer visited, then each room's name, then do the same for the second explorer. A room can be named more than once. Print four lines: how many different rooms the first explorer saw; a sorted list of every room either of them saw; a sorted list of the rooms both of them saw; and a sorted list of the rooms only the first explorer saw. Print just those four lines.
hints: Collect each explorer's rooms in a set, so a room named twice counts once. An empty set is made with set().
| gives every room in either set, & the rooms in both, and - the rooms in the first but not the second. sorted() turns each answer into a list in alphabetical order.
With other names: birds = set() goes before a loop, and birds.add(name) inside it. sorted(birds) lists them.

errorHints.text: {} is an empty dictionary, and a dictionary has no add(). Start an empty set with set().
range() needs a whole number: use int(...) on each count.
Your program asked for more replies than it gets. Each explorer's count comes just before their rooms.
Make each set before the loop that fills it, and spell its name the same way every time.
With hall, cellar and tower, and then tower and garden, the lines are 3, all four rooms, ['tower'] and ['cellar', 'hall']. & gives only the rooms in both sets.
A room named twice is still one room. A set keeps one copy, so count the set, not the replies.
When the second explorer saw no rooms, nothing is in both, and every room is one only the first explorer saw.
Check two explorers who saw different rooms: no room is in both.
Check two explorers who saw the same rooms: no room is only the first explorer's.

similarExample.note: Fruit instead of rooms: & finds what both sets share, and - what is only in the first. Your challenge builds its sets from the replies, one room at a time.

otherWays.code:
first = set()
for n in range(int(input("Rooms? "))):
    first.add(input("Room? "))
second = set()
for n in range(int(input("Rooms? "))):
    second.add(input("Room? "))
print(len(first))
print(sorted(first | second))
print(sorted(first & second))
print(sorted(first - second))
otherWays.note: int(input()) can go straight into range(), because each count is only needed once.

otherWays.code:
count = int(input("Rooms? "))
first = []
for n in range(count):
    first.append(input("Room? "))
count = int(input("Rooms? "))
second = []
for n in range(count):
    second.append(input("Room? "))
a = set(first)
b = set(second)
print(len(a))
print(sorted(a.union(b)))
print(sorted(a.intersection(b)))
print(sorted(a.difference(b)))
otherWays.note: set() turns a list into a set, dropping repeats. union(), intersection() and difference() are the method names for |, & and -.

py.u05.title: A scene you can replay
py.u05.description: Name a scene once with def, then play it as often as the story needs.
py.u05.learnTitle: Give a set of steps a name
py.u05.learn: def campfire(): followed by an indented block makes a function: a named set of steps. Nothing runs yet. campfire() on its own line calls it, and its steps run then, each time it is called.
py.u05.detail: Define a function above the line that first calls it. Calling it three times runs its steps three times, so one function replaces copied lines. The brackets matter: campfire on its own names the function but does not run it.
py.u05.example:
# A scene the adventure can replay
def campfire():
    print("The fire crackles.")
    print("Someone tells a story.")

print("Night falls.")
campfire()
campfire()
py.u05.exampleOutput:
Night falls.
The fire crackles.
Someone tells a story.
The fire crackles.
Someone tells a story.
py.u05.exampleNote: def only stores the steps. The first line printed is Night falls., because the function's lines run only when campfire() is called, here twice.
py.u05.question: If the last two lines were taken away, what would the program print?
options: Night falls. and the campfire lines once
py.u05.why: Without a call, the function's steps never run. Defining a function prints nothing.
py.u05.guided: Predict, then run: take the brackets off one campfire() call and see what changes. Then write a second function, sunrise(), and call it once at the end.
py.u05.starter: # Define crossing() and journey(), then call journey()
py.u05.challenge: Write a function called crossing() that prints three lines: Step on the stones. then The water rushes past. then You reach the far bank. Then write a function called journey() that prints Day begins., uses crossing() twice, and prints Night falls. At the end of your program, call journey() once. The check runs your program, and also calls your functions on their own.
hints: Each function starts with def, its name, empty brackets and a colon. The lines that belong to it are indented by four spaces.
journey() can call crossing() inside its own block, so the three river lines are written only once. The last line of the program, not indented, calls journey().
The same shape with other names: def chorus(): holds the lines, and def song(): calls chorus() between its own print() lines.

errorHints.text: A function has to be defined above the line that first calls it, and spelled the same way in both places.
The lines inside a function start with four spaces. The final call to journey() has none.
Run on its own, your program should print the whole journey once: eight lines. If it prints nothing, add a call to journey() at the end, with no indent.
crossing() should print exactly the three river lines, in order, and nothing else.
Check journey() on its own: it should print Day begins., the river lines twice, and Night falls.

similarExample.code:
def chorus():
    print("La la la")

def song():
    print("Verse one")
    chorus()
    print("Verse two")
    chorus()

song()
similarExample.note: A song whose chorus is written once and sung twice. Your journey does the same with the river crossing.

otherWays.note: A loop can call crossing() twice, and another can print its lines from a list.

otherWays.code:
def crossing():
    print("Step on the stones.")
    print("The water rushes past.")
    print("You reach the far bank.")

def journey():
    print("Day begins.")
    crossing()
    crossing()
    print("Night falls.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    journey()
otherWays.note: if __name__ == "__main__": runs journey() only when this file is the program being run, not when another file imports it. You will meet this again with modules.

py.u05.title: Any hero, any place
py.u05.concept: Functions · parameters, defaults and named arguments
py.u05.description: Write one scene that works for every hero and place, with a mood that has a sensible default.
py.u05.learn: def greet(name): gives the function a parameter: a name for a value it is handed. greet("Nova") calls it with the argument "Nova", so inside the function, name holds "Nova".
py.u05.detail: A function can take several parameters, matched in order: def trade(item, price):. A default, as in def trade(item, price=5):, is used when a call leaves that value out. A call can also name them, trade(price=2, item="rope"), and then their order does not matter.
py.u05.example:
# One scene, many heroes
def arrive(hero, place="the harbour"):
    print(hero + " arrives at " + place + ".")

arrive("Nova")
arrive("Kai", "the tower")
arrive(place="the mill", hero="Ada")
py.u05.exampleOutput:
Nova arrives at the harbour.
Kai arrives at the tower.
Ada arrives at the mill.
py.u05.exampleNote: The first call leaves place out, so it uses the default. The second matches its arguments in order. The third names them, so they can come in any order.
py.u05.question: What would arrive("the tower", "Kai") print?
py.u05.why: Arguments without names are matched in order: the first one becomes hero, whatever it says.
py.u05.guided: Predict, then run: swap the two arguments in the second call. Then give hero a default too, and call arrive() with no arguments at all.
py.u05.challenge: Write a function called scene(hero, place, mood="calm") that prints one line: the hero, the words is in, the place, a comma, the word feeling, and the mood, ending with a full stop. For example, scene("Nova", "the cave") prints Nova is in the cave, feeling calm. Your program should not ask for input: the check calls your functions with its own values.
hints: The def line lists three parameters, and the last one has a default: mood="calm".
Inside, build the line from the parameters, not from any one hero's name, so that every call gets its own hero and place.
The same idea with other names: def order(dish, drink="water"): can print dish + " with " + drink + "." for any dish.

errorHints.text: Check the def line: scene() takes the hero, the place and then the mood, and the mood has a default so calls may leave it out.
Inside the function, use the parameter names from the def line, spelled the same way.
With scene("Nova", "the cave") the line is Nova is in the cave, feeling calm. Check the spaces, the comma and the full stop.
A mood given in the call replaces the default: scene("Kai", "the market", "brave") feels brave.
A call can name the mood, mood="sleepy". The parameter must be called mood for that to work.
Check another hero and place: the line must come from the parameters, never from a name written into the function.
Check a call that names every argument: the parameters must be called hero, place and mood.

similarExample.code:
def order(dish, drink="water"):
    print(dish + " with " + drink + ".")

order("soup")
order("pie", "milk")
similarExample.note: A meal order with a default drink. Your scene() has two parameters before its default, and different words around them.

otherWays.code:
def scene(hero, place, mood="calm"):
    print(f"{hero} is in {place}, feeling {mood}.")
otherWays.note: An f-string puts each value straight into the sentence, with no + signs.
join() puts a space between the pieces of a list. Useful when a sentence is built from many parts.

py.u05.title: Score the guess
py.u05.description: Have the riddle keeper's scoring hand its answer back, so the rest of the game can use it.
py.u05.learn: return sends a value back to the line that called the function. With def double(n): return n * 2, the line x = double(4) stores 8. print() inside a function only shows text: the caller gets nothing it can use.
py.u05.detail: return also ends the function at once, so lines after it in the same block never run. A function with no return gives back None. return a, b gives back two values together, and low, high = pair() unpacks them into two names.
py.u05.example:
# Points for a riddle, worked out in one place
def points(tries):
    if tries == 1:
        return 10
    return 10 - tries * 2

total = points(1) + points(3)
print(total)
print(points(2))
py.u05.exampleNote: points() hands back a number, so two calls can be added together. When tries is 1 the first return ends the function, so the second return never runs.
py.u05.question: Suppose both return lines in points() were print() lines instead. What would total = points(1) + points(3) do?
py.u05.why: A function that only prints gives back None, and None + None is a TypeError. print() shows a number; return hands it back to be used.
py.u05.guided: Predict, then run: add print(points(5)) and work out the answer before you run it. Then change points() so that 5 or more tries scores 0, with one more if and return.
py.u05.starter: # Define score(secret, guess) and verdict(secret, guess)
py.u05.challenge: Write score(secret, guess), which returns 10 if the guess is right, 5 if it is no more than 2 away, 1 if it is no more than 10 away, and 0 otherwise. Then write verdict(secret, guess), which returns two values: the score, and True if the guess is too high or False if it is not. Return the answers; do not print them. Your program should not ask for input: the check calls your functions with its own values.
hints: Work out how far apart the two numbers are first, ignoring which is bigger: abs() gives a number without its minus sign, so abs(3 - 7) is 4. Then check the closest band first, and return as soon as one matches.
verdict() can call score() instead of repeating its rules, then return the score and a comparison together, separated by a comma.
The same shape with other names: def grade(mark): with if mark >= 90: return "A" first, then the lower bands, and a last return for everything else.

errorHints.text: Use the parameters from the def line inside the function, spelled the same way.
Check that each function takes two values, the secret and then the guess, and that score() returns a number in every case.
score(50, 50) should return 10. If the check says your function returned None, it printed the answer instead of returning it.
48 is exactly 2 away from 50, and no more than 2 away includes 2 itself.
verdict(20, 25) should return 1 and True together: return the score, a comma, and whether the guess is bigger.
Check a guess more than 10 away: every guess needs a score, so the function needs a return for the last band too.
Check a guess just below the secret: too high means bigger than the secret, not just different from it.

similarExample.note: Bands checked from the top, each ending the function with return. Your score() measures distance instead of marks.

otherWays.note: elif and else make it clear that exactly one band applies. verdict() reuses score().
The bands as a list of pairs: the loop returns from the first band the gap fits. Adding a band means adding a pair.

py.u05.title: The purse that must change
py.u05.description: Keep the hero's coins right by handing values in and back, instead of reaching outside a function.
py.u05.learnTitle: Names inside a function stay inside
py.u05.learn: A name given a value inside a function is local: it exists only while that call runs, and a name outside with the same spelling is a different name. A function can read a name from outside, but assigning to it inside makes a new local name.
py.u05.detail: So score = score + 1 inside a function stops with an UnboundLocalError: the function's own score has no value yet. The clean fix is to hand the value in and return the new one: score = add_point(score). A global line would work too, but it makes a function harder to test and reuse.
py.u05.example:
# Who changes the score?
score = 0

def bonus():
    score = 50
    print(score)

def add_point(points):
    return points + 1

bonus()
print(score)
score = add_point(score)
print(score)
py.u05.exampleNote: bonus() makes its own local score, which disappears when the call ends, so the outer score is still 0. add_point() is handed the score and gives back a new value, which the caller stores.
py.u05.question: What would happen if bonus() said score = score + 50 instead?
options: It prints 50, and the outer score stays 0
py.u05.why: Because bonus() assigns to score, every score inside it is local, and the local one has no value yet when score + 50 is worked out.
py.u05.guided: Predict, then run: inside bonus(), add print(score) above the assignment, and read the error. Then call add_point() three times in a row, storing the result each time.
py.u05.starter: # Define collect(coins, found) and spend(coins, price)
py.u05.challenge: Write collect(coins, found), which returns the hero's new number of coins after finding some more. Then write spend(coins, price), which returns two values: the coins left and True if there were enough to pay, or the coins unchanged and False if there were not. Neither function may change or depend on a name outside itself: hand the values in and return the answers. Your program should not ask for input: the check calls your functions with its own values.
hints: Everything each function needs arrives as a parameter, and everything it works out leaves by return. No name outside the functions is needed at all.
spend() has two outcomes: an if decides whether the coins cover the price, and each branch returns two values separated by a comma.
The same shape with other names: def eat(food, bite): return food - bite hands the new amount back, and the caller stores it with food = eat(food, 2).

errorHints.text: A function that assigns to coins makes its own local coins. Use the parameter instead, and return the new value.
Inside each function, use the parameters from its def line, spelled the same way.
collect(10, 5) should return 15: the coins handed in, plus the coins found.
spend(20, 8) should return 12 and True together.
When the price is more than the coins, nothing is paid: return the coins unchanged, and False.
Check spending every coin: having exactly the price is enough to pay.
Check an empty purse: the answer must come from the coins handed in, not from a name outside the function.

similarExample.code:
def eat(food, bite):
    return food - bite

food = 10
food = eat(food, 2)
food = eat(food, 3)
print(food)
similarExample.note: The amount goes in, a new amount comes back, and the caller stores it. Your spend() also says whether it could pay.

otherWays.note: Checking the refusal first means the normal case needs no else.

otherWays.code:
def collect(coins, found):
    total = coins
    total += found
    return total

def spend(coins, price):
    enough = coins >= price
    left = coins - price if enough else coins
    return left, enough
otherWays.note: Names made inside a function, like total and enough, are local: they cannot clash with anything outside.

py.u05.title: Break the battle into parts
py.u05.description: Adventure v2: split a fight into small functions that each do one job, and build the whole from them.
py.u05.learn: Big programs are easier to read and fix when each function does one small job and has a name that says what it is. A function that works something out returns its answer, and another function can use it.
py.u05.detail: A good test of a function: can you call it on its own, with made-up values, and check its answer? If one function reads input(), prints and changes outside names all at once, split it. Then the main part of the program just calls the parts in order.
py.u05.exampleNote: price_with_tax() is written once and used by both other functions, so a change to the tax happens in one place. Each function can be checked on its own.
py.u05.question: If the tax changed to price // 5, how many functions would need editing?
py.u05.why: Only price_with_tax() works out the tax. The others call it, so they change with it.
py.u05.guided: Predict, then run: change the tax to price // 5 and check all three answers. Then write total_cost(prices), which adds up price_with_tax() of every price in a list.
py.u05.challenge: Write three functions for the adventure's battles. damage(attack, armour) returns the attack minus the armour, but never less than 0. fight(hero_hp, attack, armour) returns the hero's health after one hit, using damage(), and never less than 0. survives(hero_hp, attacks, armour) takes a list of attack values, applies them in order with fight(), and returns True if the hero has more than 0 health at the end, or False. Your program should not ask for input: the check calls your functions with its own values.
hints: Write damage() first and check it alone: max() of two numbers picks the bigger one, which is a short way to say never less than 0.
fight() takes the damage away from the health and keeps the result from going below 0. survives() loops over the attacks list, storing what fight() returns each time.
The same layering with other names: def heal(hp, potion): returns the bigger health, and def rest(hp, potions): loops over potions, storing hp = heal(hp, p) each time.

errorHints.text: A function can call another one defined anywhere in the file, as long as the name is spelled the same way.
Check the order of the parameters in each def line, and that every function returns a value in every case.
damage(7, 3) should return 4: the attack minus the armour.
damage(2, 5) should return 0: armour stronger than the attack stops it completely, and damage is never negative.
fight(10, 6, 2) should return 6: the damage is 6 - 2, which is 4, taken off 10.
survives(10, [4, 4, 4], 1) should return True: each hit does 3, leaving 1 health.
Check a fight the hero loses: health that reaches 0 means the hero did not survive.
Check one very heavy hit: health stops at 0, it never goes below.

similarExample.note: Two layers: heal() does one potion and never goes past 20, and rest() applies a list of them with it. Your fight goes the other way, down to 0.

otherWays.note: if statements instead of max(), and survives() returns the comparison itself, which is already True or False.
survives() can stop as soon as the health reaches 0, because nothing after that can bring it back.

py.u06.title: Read the crash report
py.u06.description: The shop's ledger crashes. Read each crash report from the bottom up, and fix the line it points to.
py.u06.learnTitle: Read it from the bottom up
py.u06.learn: When Python stops, it prints a traceback. Its last line names the kind of error and says what went wrong. The line just above that says where: the line number, and the line itself.
py.u06.detail: Lines higher up show how the program got there, such as the line that called the function that failed. Start with the last line, go to the line it names, and only then read further up. This page explains an error in plain words first, and Show Python's message has the whole traceback, where your program is called "<exec>".
py.u06.example:
# Fixed: each price was text, so total + price failed
prices = ["5", "12"]
total = 0
for price in prices:
    total = total + int(price)
print(total)
py.u06.exampleNote: Before the fix, the last line of the traceback was TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str', and the line above it showed total = total + price. Turning each price into a number fixed it.
py.u06.question: A traceback ends with File "<exec>", line 7, in <module> and then NameError: name 'totl' is not defined. Where do you look first?
options: The last line of the program
py.u06.why: The line above the error names the place. Line 7 uses a name that was never given a value, probably a typo for total.
py.u06.guided: Predict, then run: take int() out again and read the error. Open Show Python's message and find the line number. Then misspell total on the print line, and compare the two messages.
py.u06.starter:
# The shop's ledger crashes. Fix it one traceback at a time.
def total_cost(prices):
    total = 0
    for i in range(len(prices) + 1):
        total = total + prices[i]
    return total

count = int(input("How many items? "))
prices = []
for n in range(count):
    prices.append(input("Price? "))
print("Total: " + total_cost(prices))
print("Most expensive: " + str(max(prices)))
py.u06.challenge: The shop's ledger in your editor asks how many items there are (always at least 1) and each item's price, then prints the total and the most expensive price, as Total: 25 and Most expensive: 12. It crashes. Run it, read each traceback from the bottom up, fix what it points to, and run again until it works. There are three bugs.
hints: Run the program and read the last line of the error first: it names the kind of error. The line number above it says where.
There are three separate bugs. Fix only what the error points to, run again, and read the next error. A program can fail inside a function because of the values the caller handed it.
With other names: when ages = ["14", "15"] holds text, sum = sum + int(age) fixes the adding, and str(sum) turns a number into text that can be joined.

errorHints.text: Python cannot add text and a number. A reply from input() is text until int() turns it into a number, and a number must be turned into text with str() before + joins it to words.
A position is past the end of the list. range(len(prices)) already gives every position; one more is one too many.
A name is used that has no value: check its spelling against the line where it was made.
With prices 5, 9 and 8, the lines are Total: 22 and Most expensive: 9.
With one price of 7, the total and the most expensive price are both 7.
With prices 9 and 10 the most expensive is 10. If you got 9, the prices were compared as text, where "9" comes after "10".
Check a longer list: every price is added, the first and the last too.
Check prices that are all the same.

similarExample.note: Text turned into numbers before comparing, and a number turned back into text to be joined. Your ledger needs both kinds of fix.

otherWays.code:
count = int(input("How many items? "))
prices = []
for n in range(count):
    prices.append(int(input("Price? ")))
print("Total: " + str(sum(prices)))
print("Most expensive: " + str(max(prices)))
otherWays.note: sum() replaces the whole total_cost() function. Fixing a bug can also mean finding a simpler way.

otherWays.code:
def total_cost(prices):
    total = 0
    for price in prices:
        total = total + price
    return total

count = int(input("How many items? "))
prices = []
for n in range(count):
    prices.append(int(input("Price? ")))
print(f"Total: {total_cost(prices)}")
print(f"Most expensive: {max(prices)}")
otherWays.note: Looping over the prices instead of their positions removes the off-by-one bug for good, and f-strings turn numbers into text for you.

py.u06.title: Wrong by one
py.u06.concept: Debugging · find the line that is wrong
py.u06.description: A tally that never crashes but gives the wrong answers. Find its bugs by testing small cases and printing what is going on.
py.u06.learnTitle: When the answer is wrong, not the program
py.u06.learn: Some bugs never crash: the program runs and prints the wrong thing. To find one, guess what each name should hold at each step, then check it with a print() inside the code.
py.u06.detail: Change one thing at a time and run again, so you know which change mattered. Try the smallest input that goes wrong, like a single round. Explaining each line out loud, even to a rubber duck, often shows the line that does not do what you meant. Take the extra print() lines out when you are done.
py.u06.example:
# Why does the countdown miss numbers?
for n in range(5, 0, -2):
    print("n is", n)
print("done")
py.u06.exampleOutput:
n is 5
n is 3
n is 1
done
py.u06.exampleNote: Printing n at every turn shows the loop goes 5, 3, 1: the step of -2 skips the numbers in between. A label like "n is" makes the extra lines easy to spot and remove later.
py.u06.question: With rounds = 3, how many times does the body of for r in range(1, rounds): run?
py.u06.why: range(1, 3) gives 1 and 2, then stops before 3: one turn fewer than there are rounds.
py.u06.guided: Predict, then run: change the step to -1 and read the printed values. Then add a second print inside the loop that shows n * 2.
py.u06.starter:
# The tally gives wrong answers, but never crashes. Find out why.
rounds = int(input("Rounds? "))
best = 0
wins = 0
for r in range(1, rounds):
    points = int(input("Points? "))
    if points > best:
        best = points
    if points > 10:
        wins = wins + 1
print(best)
print(wins)
py.u06.challenge: The tally in your editor should ask how many rounds were played (always at least 1), then the points from each round, which can be negative. It should print two lines: the best score of any round, and how many rounds were wins, where a win scores 10 or more. It runs, but its answers are wrong. Find and fix its three bugs.
hints: Run it with one round of 15 points. One round should give 15 and 1; what do you get instead? That small case shows the first bug.
Put print("round", r, "points", points) inside the loop to watch each turn. Check three things: how many rounds are read, what counts as a win, and where best starts.
With other names: when the first value must count even if it is negative, start lowest = None and check if lowest is None or temp < lowest: before storing lowest = temp.

errorHints.text: A name was used that has no value yet: check its spelling against the line where it was made.
If best starts as None, check for None before comparing: None > 5 is an error.
Your loop asked for more points than there were rounds. range(rounds) runs exactly once per round.
With 4, 12 and 10 points, the best is 12 and there are 2 wins: 10 counts as a win.
With one round of 15, the answers are 15 and 1. If you got 0 and 0, the loop never ran: count how many numbers range(1, 1) gives.
With -3 and -1, the best score is -1. A best that starts at 0 is already higher than every score here.
Check a longer game, counting every round that scores 10 or more.
Check scores just below, at and above 10.

similarExample.code:
temps = [3, -2, 5]
lowest = None
for temp in temps:
    print("checking", temp, "lowest so far", lowest)
    if lowest is None or temp < lowest:
        lowest = temp
print(lowest)
similarExample.note: A debugging print shows each step, and lowest starts as None so even the first value counts. Your tally looks for the highest score instead.

otherWays.code:
rounds = int(input("Rounds? "))
best = None
wins = 0
for r in range(rounds):
    points = int(input("Points? "))
    if best is None or points > best:
        best = points
    if points >= 10:
        wins += 1
print(best)
print(wins)
otherWays.note: best starts as None, meaning nothing yet, so the first round always counts.
Keeping every score in a list lets max() find the best, so there is no starting value to get wrong.

py.u06.title: A safe share
py.u06.description: Share the coins without crashing, whatever the player types.
py.u06.learnTitle: Catch an error before it stops the program
py.u06.learn: Code inside try: runs as usual. If one of its lines raises an error that an except names, Python jumps to that except block instead of stopping. int("seven") raises a ValueError, so except ValueError: catches it.
py.u06.detail: Name the error you expect. A bare except: catches every error, even a typing mistake of your own, and hides it. else: runs when nothing went wrong, and finally: runs either way. Keep the try block short, so you know which lines it protects.
py.u06.exampleOutput:
5
not a number
nobody to share with
py.u06.exampleNote: Each reply gets its own try. "zero" fails inside int() and jumps to the ValueError block. 0 gets through int() but fails at the division, so the other block catches it.
py.u06.question: What would happen with the reply "4.5"?
py.u06.why: int() only reads whole numbers, so "4.5" raises a ValueError, which the first except catches.
py.u06.guided: Predict, then run: add "4.5" and "-3" to the replies. Then take out the ZeroDivisionError block and see what happens to the 0.
py.u06.starter: # Read both replies, and share the coins safely
py.u06.challenge: Ask how many coins there are, then how many friends share them. Print each friend's share, using //, and then the coins left over, using %. If either reply is not a whole number, print just not a number instead. If there are 0 friends, print just nobody to share with instead.
hints: Put the lines that can fail, the two int() calls and the sharing, inside one try: block.
Add one except block for each kind of error you expect: a reply that is not a whole number, and a share among 0 friends. Each one prints its own message.
With other names: try: with n = int(reply) inside it, then except ValueError: with print("try again") inside that.

errorHints.text: int() could not read a reply. Put the int() lines inside try:, and add an except ValueError: block.
Sharing among 0 friends raises a ZeroDivisionError. Catch it with an except block of its own.
The lines inside try: and inside each except: start with four spaces.
With 60 coins and 7 friends, each gets 8 and 4 are left over.
When the coins are typed as a word, the program prints only not a number.
With 0 friends the program prints only nobody to share with, and no share.
Check a number of friends that is not a whole number.
Check a number of coins with a decimal point: int() refuses it.

similarExample.note: One kind of error caught for two replies. Your share needs two except blocks, because two different things can go wrong.

otherWays.note: else: runs only when the try block raised nothing, so the printing is kept apart from the lines that can fail.
An if can check for 0 before dividing. try suits errors you cannot easily check first, like text that may not be a number.

py.u06.title: Rules of the game
py.u06.description: Make a function refuse a value that breaks the rules, with a message that says why.
py.u06.learnTitle: Refuse a value that breaks the rules
py.u06.learn: raise ValueError("guess must be from 1 to 100") stops a function with that error and message, just as int("x") stops with one of its own. The code that called it can catch it with try and except, and read the message.
py.u06.detail: Raise an error that fits: ValueError for a value of the right kind but a bad amount, TypeError for the wrong kind of value. except ValueError as error: gives the caught error a name, and printing it shows its message. Raising early, at the top of a function, keeps the rest of it simple.
py.u06.exampleOutput:
50
Refused: guess must be from 1 to 100
py.u06.exampleNote: 50 passes the check and comes back. 200 makes check_guess() raise, so the print never happens, and the except prints the message instead.
py.u06.question: What would check_guess(0) do if nothing caught the error?
options: Stop the program with a ValueError
py.u06.why: Nothing catches it, so the error stops the program, just like any other ValueError.
py.u06.guided: Predict, then run: add 0 and 100 to the list. Then make check_guess() also refuse odd numbers, with a message of your own.
py.u06.starter: # Define set_lives(lives), then use it with the reply
py.u06.challenge: Write a function set_lives(lives) that returns lives if it is from 1 to 9, and otherwise raises a ValueError with the message lives must be from 1 to 9. Then ask the player for a number of lives, as a whole number, and pass it to set_lives() inside a try: print the lives it returns, or, if a ValueError is raised, print Refused: followed by a space and the message.
hints: In set_lives(), check the rule first, and raise the error when it is broken. If the function gets past that check, the lives are fine to return.
Call set_lives() inside try:. except ValueError as error: catches the error you raised, and error holds its message.
With other names: def set_speed(speed): can raise ValueError("speed must be positive") when speed < 0 is True, and print("Slow down:", error) shows the message.

errorHints.text: An error stopped the program without being caught. Call set_lives() inside try:, with an except ValueError as error: block.
Check the function is called set_lives everywhere, and that error is the name given in the except line.
With 5 lives, the program prints just 5.
With 12 lives, it prints Refused: lives must be from 1 to 9, the message coming from the error you raised.
set_lives(3) should return 3. If it returned None, it printed instead of returning.
Check 0 lives: fewer than 1 breaks the rule too.
Check the edges of the rule: 1 and 9 are both allowed.
Check a negative number of lives.

similarExample.note: Another rule, refused with a message and caught by the caller. Your lives rule has two edges, not one.

otherWays.note: A chained comparison checks both edges at once. Here int() is inside the try too, so a word would be refused with int()'s own message.
range(1, 10) holds exactly the numbers 1 to 9. else: prints only when nothing was raised.

py.u06.title: Ask until it is right
py.u06.concept: Input · asking again until the reply is valid
py.u06.description: The bridge keeper keeps asking until the reply makes sense, and says what was wrong each time.
py.u06.learnTitle: Keep asking until the reply makes sense
py.u06.learn: A while True: loop can ask again and again. Inside it, try to turn the reply into a number; when that works and the number is in range, break leaves the loop. Otherwise, say what was wrong, and the loop asks again.
py.u06.detail: Every path through the loop must either break or ask again, or the loop never ends. An empty reply is text too: int("") raises a ValueError. continue jumps straight back to the top of the loop. On this page, if the replies run out, input() raises an EOFError, which means the program asked more times than it was answered.
py.u06.exampleOutput:
Type a number.
There are only 3 doors.
You open door 2
py.u06.exampleNote: continue goes straight back to the top to ask again, and break leaves the loop for good. The loop ends only on a reply that passes both checks.
py.u06.question: If the replies were an empty one and then 3, what would print first?
py.u06.why: An empty reply is still text, and int("") raises a ValueError.
py.u06.guided: Predict, then run: make the replies an empty one and then 3. Then change the range to 1 to 5, and try 5.
py.u06.starter: # Keep asking until the reply is a whole number from 1 to 8
py.u06.challenge: The bridge keeper asks how many travellers are crossing, from 1 to 8. Keep asking until the reply is a whole number from 1 to 8. For a reply that is not a whole number, print not a number. For a whole number outside 1 to 8, print from 1 to 8 only. Once a reply is valid, print how many replies it took, counting the good one, and then the number of travellers.
hints: A while True: loop asks once per turn. Count the turns with a number that starts at 0 above the loop.
Inside the loop, try int() on the reply. A ValueError means not a number; a number outside the range gets the other message; anything else is good, and break leaves the loop.
With other names: while True: then age = int(input()) inside a try:, and if 1 <= age <= 120: then break.

errorHints.text: int() could not read a reply. Put it inside try:, and print not a number in the except ValueError: block.
Give each name a value before it is used, and spell it the same way every time, such as the count of replies.
Your loop asked again after a good reply. When the reply is valid, break out of the loop.
A good first reply of 3 gives 1 and 3: one reply, three travellers.
With many, 12 and 8: not a number, from 1 to 8 only, then 3 replies and 8 travellers. 8 is allowed.
An empty reply is not a number either. Count it as a reply.
Check 0, which is a whole number but not from 1 to 8.
Check a number with a decimal point, and a negative one.

similarExample.note: The same checks over a fixed list of replies. Your bridge keeper asks with input() instead, for as long as it takes, and counts the replies.

otherWays.note: isdigit() checks the text before int() is used, so no try is needed. lstrip("-") lets a negative number through to the range check.
The loop can run while there is no answer yet, instead of while True with break.

py.u07.title: The toolbox
py.u07.description: Borrow ready-made tools from Python's math module to measure the round tower.
py.u07.learnTitle: Borrow tools that are already made
py.u07.learn: import math loads Python's math module, and math.sqrt(16) uses one of its tools: the module's name, a dot, then the tool. from math import sqrt brings in just that tool, so you can write sqrt(16).
py.u07.detail: import math as m gives the module a shorter name. Once imported, a module stays loaded for the rest of the program. On this page only some modules can be imported: math, random, datetime, json, csv and re. Asking for any other, such as os, stops with a ModuleNotFoundError that says it is not available here.
py.u07.example:
# Three ways to reach a tool
import math
from math import floor
import math as m

print(math.sqrt(49))
print(floor(7.9))
print(m.pi > 3)
py.u07.exampleNote: math.sqrt() names the module each time. floor came in on its own, so it needs no math. in front. m is just another name for the same module.
py.u07.question: What does print(sqrt(49)) do in a program that only has import math?
py.u07.why: import math brings in the module, not each of its tools by itself: the tool is math.sqrt. from math import sqrt would make sqrt work on its own.
py.u07.guided: Predict, then run: try print(sqrt(49)) with only import math. Then add import os and read the message.
py.u07.starter: # Import what you need, then measure the tower
py.u07.challenge: Ask for the radius of a round tower, as a whole number. Print three lines: the distance around it, which is 2 times pi times the radius, rounded to 1 decimal place (round(x, 1) does that); the area inside it, pi times the radius times the radius, rounded to 1 decimal place; and how many steps of length 1 it takes to walk all the way round, rounded up to a whole step. Use pi and ceil() from the math module: ceil() rounds a number up to the next whole number, so ceil(4.1) is 5.
hints: The math module has pi, to many more decimal places than 3.14, and a tool that rounds a number up.
round(x, 1) keeps one decimal place. The steps are the distance around rounded up, so even a little extra is one more step.
With other names, for a square pen: import math, then edge = 4 * side, and math.ceil(edge / 3) is how many fence panels of length 3 it needs.

errorHints.text: math is a name only after import math at the top of the program. A tool brought in with from math import ... is used without math. in front.
Turn the radius reply into a number with int(...) before working with it.
With a radius of 1: 6.3 around, 3.1 inside, and 7 steps, because 6.28... rounds up to 7.
With a radius of 10 the area is 314.2. If you got 314.0, pi was 3.14: use math.pi.
A radius of 0 gives 0.0, 0.0 and 0 steps.
Check another radius: every answer comes from the reply.
Check a radius whose distance around rounds to a whole number of tenths.

similarExample.code:
import math
side = 2.5
edge = 4 * side
print(edge)
print(math.ceil(edge / 3))
print(round(math.pi, 3))
similarExample.note: A square pen instead of a round tower: the math module's ceil() rounds the panels up. Your tower needs pi as well.

otherWays.code:
from math import pi, ceil
radius = int(input("Radius? "))
around = 2 * pi * radius
print(round(around, 1))
print(round(pi * radius ** 2, 1))
print(ceil(around))
otherWays.note: from math import brings in pi and ceil by name, so they need no math. in front. ** 2 squares the radius.

otherWays.code:
import math as m
radius = int(input("Radius? "))
print(round(m.tau * radius, 1))
print(round(m.pi * m.pow(radius, 2), 1))
print(m.ceil(m.tau * radius))
otherWays.note: tau is 2 times pi, and the math module has it too. as m is a shorter name for the module.

py.u07.title: The riddle keeper's dice
py.u07.concept: random · seed, randint, choice and shuffle
py.u07.description: Roll the riddle keeper's dice, and learn why a seed makes chance repeatable.
py.u07.learn: import random gives a program chance. random.randint(1, 6) picks a whole number from 1 to 6, both included. random.choice(paths) picks one item from a list, and random.shuffle(cards) mixes a list in place.
py.u07.detail: The numbers only look random: they are worked out from a starting number called a seed. random.seed(7) at the start makes every run give the same numbers, which is how games are tested and how this page checks your program. Without a seed, each run differs.
py.u07.example:
# The same seed gives the same "random" story every time
import random
random.seed(7)
print(random.randint(1, 6))
print(random.choice(["left", "right", "up"]))
cards = ["sun", "moon", "star"]
random.shuffle(cards)
print(cards)
py.u07.exampleNote: With the seed set to 7, these three lines come out the same on every run, on any computer with the same Python.
py.u07.question: If the program ran again with the same seed, what would it print?
py.u07.why: A seed fixes where the numbers start, so the same seed gives the same numbers in the same order.
py.u07.guided: Predict, then run it twice: the same lines both times. Then take out random.seed(7) and run it a few times.
py.u07.starter: # Import random, then roll each die
py.u07.challenge: The riddle keeper rolls dice. Ask for the number of dice and the number of sides each one has. Roll every die with random.randint(), from 1 to the number of sides, and print each roll on its own line, then the total of all the rolls on the last line. Do not call random.seed() yourself: the check sets the seed, so its numbers match yours.
hints: Import random at the top. A for loop over range() rolls once per die.
Each roll is random.randint(1, sides): store it, print it, and add it to a total that starts at 0 before the loop.
With other names: coin = random.randint(0, 1) flips a coin, and heads = heads + coin counts the heads.

errorHints.text: random is a name only after import random, at the top of the program.
randint() and range() need whole numbers: turn each reply into one with int(...).
If your rolls differ from the ones shown, check that you did not call random.seed() yourself, and that each die is rolled once, with randint(1, sides), in order.
A die with 20 sides rolls from 1 to 20: the second number in randint() is the number of sides.
With three two-sided dice, each roll is 1 or 2, and the last line adds them up.
Check many dice: one roll per die, and the total of them all at the end.
Check a die with only one side: it always rolls 1.

similarExample.code:
import random
random.seed(1)
heads = 0
for flip in range(4):
    coin = random.randint(0, 1)
    heads = heads + coin
print(heads)
similarExample.note: Four coin flips with a fixed seed, counting heads. Your dice print every roll as well as the total.

otherWays.code:
from random import randint
dice = int(input("Dice? "))
sides = int(input("Sides? "))
rolls = []
for n in range(dice):
    rolls.append(randint(1, sides))
for roll in rolls:
    print(roll)
print(sum(rolls))
otherWays.note: Keep the rolls in a list first, then print them and add them up with sum().

otherWays.code:
import random
dice = int(input("Dice? "))
sides = int(input("Sides? "))
total = 0
while dice > 0:
    roll = random.randrange(1, sides + 1)
    print(roll)
    total += roll
    dice -= 1
print(total)
otherWays.note: randrange() stops just before its second number, so randrange(1, sides + 1) picks from the same numbers as randint(1, sides), and gives the same rolls.

py.u07.title: As the crow flies
py.u07.concept: math · roots, rounding and nearly-equal numbers
py.u07.description: Measure how far the treasure is in a straight line, and round the answers honestly.
py.u07.learnTitle: Rounding, roots, and numbers that are nearly equal
py.u07.learn: math.sqrt() finds a square root, and math.hypot(a, b) the long side of a right-angled triangle. math.floor() rounds down, math.ceil() rounds up, and round(x, 2) rounds to 2 decimal places.
py.u07.detail: Decimal numbers are stored in binary, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. Compare such numbers with math.isclose(a, b), or round them before printing. round() rounds a number that is exactly half way to the nearest even number, so round(2.5) is 2.
py.u07.example:
import math
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))
print(math.floor(-2.5), math.ceil(-2.5))
print(round(2.5), round(3.5))
print(math.hypot(3, 4))
py.u07.exampleNote: 0.1 + 0.2 is very slightly more than 0.3, and isclose() allows for that. floor() and ceil() go down and up even for negative numbers, and round() picks the even neighbour for a half.
py.u07.question: What does print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3) show?
py.u07.why: == compares exactly, and 0.1 + 0.2 is stored as 0.30000000000000004. isclose() is the honest test for decimals.
py.u07.guided: Predict, then run: try round(0.5) and round(1.5). Then print math.sqrt(2), and round it to 3 places.
py.u07.starter: # Import math, then measure the way to the treasure
py.u07.challenge: The treasure lies on the map grid. Ask how many squares east it is, then how many north, as whole numbers (either can be 0). Print three lines: the straight-line distance to it, rounded to 2 decimal places; how many squares the hero walks if they can only move along the grid, east plus north; and the straight-line distance rounded up to a whole number.
hints: The straight-line distance is the square root of east squared plus north squared, or math.hypot(east, north) in one step.
round(x, 2) keeps two decimal places, and math.ceil() rounds up. The grid walk needs no square roots at all.
With other names: import math, then side = math.sqrt(area) and boxes = math.ceil(items / 6).

errorHints.text: math is a name only after import math at the top of the program.
Turn the replies into numbers with int(...) before working with them.
With 3 east and 4 north: 5.0 in a straight line, 7 along the grid, and 5 rounded up.
With 1 east and 1 north the distance is the square root of 2, so the first line is 1.41 and the last is 2.
Straight north, the distance is just the number north, as a decimal: 6.0.
Check a longer walk: round to 2 places, and round up for the last line, even when the decimal part is small.
Check a treasure at the start: everything is 0.

similarExample.code:
import math
area = 50
side = math.sqrt(area)
print(round(side, 1))
print(math.ceil(side))
similarExample.note: A square plot of 50: its side is a square root, rounded two ways. Your treasure needs the root of two squares added together.

otherWays.code:
import math
east = int(input("East? "))
north = int(input("North? "))
distance = math.hypot(east, north)
print(round(distance, 2))
print(east + north)
print(math.ceil(distance))
otherWays.note: hypot() works out the straight-line distance in one step.

otherWays.code:
from math import ceil
east = int(input("East? "))
north = int(input("North? "))
distance = (east ** 2 + north ** 2) ** 0.5
print(round(distance, 2))
print(east + north)
print(ceil(distance))
otherWays.note: ** 0.5 is a square root too. Only ceil() is needed from math.

py.u07.title: A study schedule
py.u07.description: Plan study sessions on real calendar dates, across month ends and leap days, and spot the weekends.
py.u07.learnTitle: Work with dates, not just numbers
py.u07.learn: from datetime import date gives a tool for calendar dates: date(2026, 3, 1) is the first of March 2026. Taking one date from another gives a timedelta, and its .days says how many days apart they are.
py.u07.detail: Adding timedelta(days=10) to a date moves it 10 days on, across month and year ends, and through 29 February in a leap year. .weekday() gives 0 for Monday up to 6 for Sunday, and .isoformat() writes a date as 2026-03-01, which is also how print() shows it. Checks here never read today's date, because it changes: they use fixed dates.
py.u07.example:
from datetime import date, timedelta
start = date(2026, 2, 20)
exam = date(2026, 3, 6)
print((exam - start).days)
print(start + timedelta(days=10))
print(exam.weekday())
py.u07.exampleNote: 2026 is not a leap year, so February has 28 days. Adding 10 days to 20 February lands in March, and weekday() 4 means Friday.
py.u07.question: How many days are there from date(2028, 2, 20) to date(2028, 3, 6)?
py.u07.why: 2028 is a leap year, so February has a 29th day, one more than in 2026.
py.u07.guided: Predict, then run: change both years to 2028. Then print the weekday of your own birthday this year.
py.u07.starter: # Read the start date, then list the sessions
py.u07.challenge: Plan study sessions. Ask for a start date as three whole numbers, the year, the month and the day, then how many sessions there are and how many days apart they are. Print the date of every session, starting with the start date, one per line, in the form 2026-03-02. On the last line, print how many of the sessions fall on a Saturday or a Sunday.
hints: Make the start date with date(year, month, day), after turning the replies into whole numbers.
Each session is the start plus a timedelta of days: the session number times the gap. weekday() gives 5 for Saturday and 6 for Sunday.
With other names: lesson = first + timedelta(days=7 * week) gives a weekly lesson, and lesson.weekday() >= 5 says whether it falls on a weekend.

errorHints.text: date and timedelta are names only after from datetime import date, timedelta at the top.
date() and timedelta() need whole numbers: turn each reply into one with int(...).
date() refused a date that does not exist, such as month 13 or 30 February. Check the order: year, then month, then day.
Three sessions a week apart from Monday 2 March 2026 are 2, 9 and 16 March, and none is at a weekend.
Adding days carries across the end of a month for you: 30 January plus 2 days is 1 February.
One session is just the start date, and the last line counts whether it is at a weekend.
Check a leap year: 2028 has a 29 February.
Check sessions on every day of a week.

similarExample.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta
first = date(2026, 9, 7)
for week in range(3):
    lesson = first + timedelta(days=7 * week)
    print(lesson, lesson.weekday() >= 5)
similarExample.note: Weekly lessons from a fixed first date, each with whether it falls at a weekend. Your schedule counts the weekends at the end.

otherWays.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta
start = date(int(input()), int(input()), int(input()))
sessions = int(input())
step = timedelta(days=int(input()))
day = start
weekend = 0
for n in range(sessions):
    print(day)

py.u07.title: A helper file
py.u07.description: Quiz tool v1: keep the grading rules in a file of their own, and use them from the main program.
py.u07.learn: A file of your own, such as helpers.py, is a module too. import helpers runs it once and lets the program use what it defines, as helpers.greet("Nova"). from helpers import greet brings in one name.
py.u07.detail: Keep the tools in the helper file and the story in main.py. A module's top-level lines run when it is imported, so a helper file should mostly hold definitions. On this page a file can't take the name of one of Python's own modules, such as random.py, and files are not saved between runs.
py.u07.example:

from shop import price_with_tax

print(shop.receipt("rope", 20))
print(price_with_tax(50))
py.u07.exampleNote: main.py reaches receipt() through the module name, and price_with_tax() by itself, because from brought it in by name. The tools are written once, in shop.py.
py.u07.question: If shop.py also had print("shop ready") at its top level, when would that line print?
options: Every time a shop function is called
py.u07.why: A module's top-level lines run once, the first time it is imported. Calling its functions later runs only the functions.
py.u07.guided: Predict, then run: add print("shop ready") to shop.py, then import shop twice in main.py and count the lines it prints.

py.u08.title: Test the scorer
py.u08.description: Write tests that prove the streak bonus works, and that catch it when it doesn't.
py.u08.learnTitle: Write down what should be true
py.u08.learn: assert total == 15 does nothing when it is true. When it is false, it stops the program with an AssertionError. A list of asserts is a test: it checks that code gives the answers you expect.
py.u08.detail: Test a function by calling it with values you have worked out by hand: assert add_points(2, 3) == 5. A test that can never fail, such as assert True, checks nothing. A message after a comma explains a failure: assert lives > 0, "out of lives".
py.u08.example:
# Tests for a tiny scorer
def points(guess, secret):
    if guess == secret:
        return 10
    return 0

assert points(4, 4) == 10
assert points(3, 4) == 0
print("all tests passed")
py.u08.exampleNote: Both asserts are true, so the program reaches the print. If points() had a bug, an assert would stop the program, and the print would never run.
py.u08.question: What would happen if the first assert said assert points(4, 4) == 5?
py.u08.why: points(4, 4) is 10, so the assert is false and stops the program. The test itself was wrong here, not points(): a failing test can mean either.
py.u08.guided: Predict, then run: change the 10 to 5 in the first assert and read the error. Then break points() itself, by making it return 1, and see which assert notices.
py.u08.starter: # Write asserts that test bonus(points, streak)
py.u08.challenge: The check has a function bonus(points, streak) that doubles the points when the streak is 3 or more, and otherwise returns the points unchanged. Write asserts that test bonus(). The check runs your tests on a correct bonus(), where they must all pass, and on broken versions, where at least one must fail. Do not write bonus() yourself: the check provides it.
hints: Each test calls bonus() with values you choose, and compares the answer with one you worked out by hand: assert, the call, ==, and the answer.
Test both sides of the rule: a streak below 3, a streak of exactly 3, and one above it. Use more than one number of points too.
With other names: for a function half(n), assert half(10) == 5 checks a typical value, and assert half(0) == 0 checks an edge.

errorHints.text: A test failed on the correct bonus(). Work the answer out again by hand: is the value after == right?
bonus() takes two values: the points, then the streak.
The check provides bonus(): spell it exactly that way, and do not define or import it.
Your tests passed on a bonus() that never doubles. Add a test with a streak of 3 or more.
Your tests passed on a bonus() that only doubles from a streak of 4. Test a streak of exactly 3.
Your tests passed on a bonus() that always doubles. Test a short streak too, where the points stay the same.
Your tests passed on a broken bonus(). Try your tests with more than one number of points.

assert half(0) == 0
assert half(7) == 3
print("half() passed")

otherWays.note: A table of cases checked in a loop. The message after the comma says which case failed.

    assert bonus(4, 3) == 8
    assert bonus(9, 10) == 18

test_bonus()

py.u08.title: Choose good cases
py.u08.concept: Testing · typical, edge and unusual cases
py.u08.description: Pick the test cases a careless average() would trip on: empty lists, decimals, and the last score.
py.u08.learnTitle: Pick the cases a bug would trip on
py.u08.learn: One test with an easy value catches few bugs. Good tests mix a typical case, the edges, such as an empty list, a single item or a zero, and unusual values, such as negative numbers.
py.u08.detail: Work out the right answer for each case by hand before running anything. Ask what a careless version might get wrong, such as dividing with //, skipping the last item, or crashing on an empty list, and pick a case that would show it. For decimals, pick numbers whose answer is exact, such as 7 / 2 = 3.5.
py.u08.exampleOutput: typical, negative and single cases pass
py.u08.exampleNote: Three kinds of case: a typical list, all negative numbers, and a single item. Each one could catch a different bug.
py.u08.question: Which case would show the bug if best started at 0 instead of numbers[0]?
py.u08.why: With all negative numbers, none is bigger than 0, so a best that starts at 0 would wrongly return 0.
py.u08.guided: Predict, then run: change best = numbers[0] to best = 0 and see which assert fails. Then add a test for biggest([]) and read the error: what should an empty list give?
py.u08.challenge: The check has a function average(scores) that returns the average of a list of numbers, or 0 for an empty list. Write asserts that test it well. The check runs them on a correct average(), where they must all pass, and on several broken ones, where at least one must fail for each. Do not write average() yourself.
hints: Start with a typical list whose average you can work out by hand, such as [2, 4], then add the edges.
Which lists would a careless average() get wrong? An empty one, one whose average is not a whole number, and one where the last score makes a difference.
With other names: for total(prices), assert total([]) == 0 tests the empty edge, and assert total([1, 2]) == 3 a typical case.

errorHints.text: A test failed on the correct average(). Work the answer out again by hand, as a decimal: the average of 3 and 4 is 3.5.
average() takes one list: average([2, 4]), with square brackets.
The check provides average(): spell it exactly that way, and do not define it yourself.
Your tests passed on an average() that crashes on an empty list. Test the empty list, [].
Your tests passed on an average() that divides with //. Test a list whose average is not a whole number.
Your tests passed on a broken average(). Check that a change to the last score changes your answer.
Your tests passed on a broken average(). Test lists with more than one score.

def total(prices):
    result = 0
    for p in prices:
        result = result + p
    return result

assert total([]) == 0
assert total([1, 2]) == 3
assert total([5]) == 5
print("total() passed")

assert average([2, 4]) == 3
assert average([3, 4]) == 3.5

py.u08.title: Edges of the rule
py.u08.description: The ferry charges by age. Test right at the edges of each price, where off-by-one bugs hide.
py.u08.learn: A rule like "children from 5 to 12 pay 5" has edges: 4 and 5, then 12 and 13. Off-by-one bugs, such as < where <= was meant, change the answer only right at an edge.
py.u08.detail: For every edge, test the value on each side of it. Testing 8 and 30 says little about whether 12 counts as a child. 0 and 1, an empty list and a one-item list, and the first and last positions are edges too.
py.u08.example:
def can_ride(height):
    return height >= 120

assert can_ride(119) == False
assert can_ride(120) == True
assert can_ride(121) == True
print("both sides of 120 tested")
py.u08.exampleNote: 119 and 120 sit either side of the edge, and 121 is just past it. A bug in >= would show up in one of the first two.
py.u08.question: If can_ride() said height > 120, which assert would fail?
py.u08.why: Only exactly 120 is treated differently by > and >=, so only the test right on the edge notices.
py.u08.guided: Predict, then run: change >= to > and check. Then add a second rule, height <= 200, and test both sides of 200.
py.u08.challenge: The ferry has a function ticket_price(age) in the check: under 5 travel free, ages 5 to 12 pay 5, ages 13 to 64 pay 10, and 65 and over pay 6. Write asserts that test it, especially at the edges. The check runs your tests on the correct ticket_price(), where they must all pass, and on broken versions, where at least one must fail for each. Do not write ticket_price() yourself.
hints: List the edges first: where does each price start and stop? Each edge needs a test on both sides of it.
The rule has three edges, at 5, at 13 and at 65. A test on the last age of one price and the first age of the next catches a bug at that edge.
With other names: for a rule that 120 and over may ride, assert can_ride(119) == False and assert can_ride(120) == True test both sides of its edge.

errorHints.text: A test failed on the correct ticket_price(). Read the rule again: from 5 to 12 includes both 5 and 12.
ticket_price() takes one whole number, the age.
The check provides ticket_price(): spell it exactly that way.
Your tests passed on a ticket_price() that lets 5-year-olds travel free. Test age 5.
Your tests passed on a ticket_price() that charges 12-year-olds the full price. Test age 12.
Your tests passed on a ticket_price() with a broken edge. Test the ages on both sides of every edge.
Your tests passed on a ticket_price() with a broken edge. Check the edge between children and the full price from both sides.

similarExample.code:
def can_ride(height):
    return height >= 120

assert can_ride(119) == False
assert can_ride(120) == True
print("edge tested")
similarExample.note: One edge, tested on both sides. Your ticket rule has three edges.

otherWays.note: A dictionary of edge ages and their prices, checked in a loop.

py.u08.title: Labels for values
py.u08.concept: Type hints · saying what a function takes and gives
py.u08.description: Label what goes into the coin-sharing function and what comes out, so anyone reading it knows how to use it.
py.u08.learnTitle: Say what kind of value goes where
py.u08.learn: def tip(bill: float, percent: int) -> float: tells a reader that bill is a decimal number, percent a whole number, and that the function gives back a decimal. These hints are for people and tools: Python does not check them when the program runs.
py.u08.detail: Common hints are int, float, str, bool, list[int] for a list of whole numbers, and dict[str, int]. A name can have one too: lives: int = 3. Because Python ignores hints while running, a call such as twice("ha") is not stopped by them. A function's hints are kept in its __annotations__, which you can print.
py.u08.exampleNote: tip() is used as its hints say. twice() says it takes a whole number, but Python runs it with text anyway, because hints describe and do not check.
py.u08.question: What does twice("ha") do?
py.u08.why: The hint says int, but nothing checks it: "ha" * 2 is "haha", so that is what comes back.
py.u08.guided: Predict, then run: call twice(3). Then give twice() honest hints for text, word: str and -> str, and run it again.
py.u08.starter: # Define shares() with type hints, then print its __annotations__
py.u08.challenge: Write shares(coins: int, friends: int) -> list[int], with exactly those hints, which returns a list of how many coins each friend gets, shared as evenly as possible: everyone gets coins // friends, and the first coins % friends friends get one more. At the end of your program, print(shares.__annotations__) so the check can read your hints. Do not ask for input.
hints: The def line carries the hints: a colon and a type after each parameter, then -> and the return type before the final colon.
Every friend gets coins // friends, and the first coins % friends of them get one more. Build the list with a loop over range(friends).
With other names: def split(total: int, parts: int) -> list[int]: starts a function, and base = total // parts is everyone's share before the extras.

errorHints.text: Hints use the type names int and list, spelled in lowercase, and the function must be called shares.
Every call in the check has at least one friend, so check the order of the two parameters: coins first, then friends.
Check that shares() takes two whole numbers and returns a list.
Your program's last line should print shares.__annotations__, showing int for both parameters and list[int] for what it returns.
shares(12, 3) should return [4, 4, 4].
shares(14, 4) should return [4, 4, 3, 3]: two coins are left over, so the first two friends get one more.
Check fewer coins than friends: some friends get 0.
Check a single friend, who gets every coin.

similarExample.code:
def label(name: str, age: int) -> str:
    return name + " (" + str(age) + ")"

print(label("Ada", 15))
print(label.__annotations__)
similarExample.note: Hints on a function that joins text, and its __annotations__ printed. Your shares() takes two whole numbers and returns a list.

otherWays.code:
def shares(coins: int, friends: int) -> list[int]:
    base, extra = divmod(coins, friends)
    return [base + 1 if n < extra else base for n in range(friends)]

print(shares.__annotations__)
otherWays.note: divmod() gives // and % together, and the list is built in one line.
Dealing the coins out one at a time, like cards, gives the same shares. The list name carries a hint too.

py.u08.title: Tidy without breaking
py.u08.description: The shop's till works but repeats itself. Tidy it into a price list and one function, without changing a single line it prints.
py.u08.learnTitle: Change the shape, keep the behaviour
py.u08.learn: Refactoring means rewriting code so it is easier to read and change, while it does exactly what it did before. Repeated lines become one function, and values scattered through the code become one dictionary.
py.u08.detail: Work in small steps, and run the program after each one, comparing its output with what it printed before. Tests are a safety net: if they pass before and after, the behaviour has not changed. Leave new features for later, because mixing them in makes a mistake hard to find.
py.u08.example:
# Before: the same rule written three times
# print(4 * 3 + 2)
# print(7 * 3 + 2)
# print(9 * 3 + 2)

# After: one function, used three times
def stamps(pages):
    return pages * 3 + 2

for pages in [4, 7, 9]:
    print(stamps(pages))
py.u08.exampleNote: The commented lines show the program before: one rule, written three times. After, the rule lives in stamps(), and the output is exactly the same.
py.u08.question: If the rule changed to 4 stamps a page, how many places would change in the After version?
py.u08.why: The rule is written once, inside stamps(). That is the point of the refactor.
py.u08.guided: Predict, then run: change the 3 to 4. Then add assert stamps(1) == 5 above the loop, so the rule is tested, and run it again.
py.u08.starter:
# Works, but repeats itself. Tidy it without changing what it prints.
orders = int(input("How many orders? "))
total = 0
for n in range(orders):
    item = input("Item? ")
    amount = int(input("Amount? "))
    if item == "bread":
        print(item, amount * 3)
        total = total + amount * 3
    elif item == "milk":
        print(item, amount * 2)
        total = total + amount * 2
    elif item == "apple":
        print(item, amount * 1)
        total = total + amount * 1
    else:
        print(item, 0)
print("total", total)
py.u08.challenge: The till in your editor works, but each price is written three times. Tidy it: keep the prices in one dictionary, write a function cost(item, amount) that returns the cost of one order (0 for anything the shop does not sell), and use cost() in the loop. Your program must print exactly what it prints now. The check runs it with orders, and calls cost() on its own.

cost() looks the item up with get() and a default of 0, and multiplies by the amount. Then the loop calls cost() once per order, prints, and adds to the total.
With other names: rates = {"walk": 1, "ride": 4} and def fee(kind, hours): returns rates.get(kind, 0) * hours.

An item the shop does not sell is not a key in the dictionary. get(item, 0) gives 0 instead of an error.

With bread 2, milk 1 and apple 5, the lines are bread 6, milk 2, apple 5 and total 13, exactly as before.

Check cost() for something the shop does not sell.

py.u09.title: The save file
py.u09.concept: Files · open, read and write text
py.u09.description: Read the scores the game saved, line by line, and write a summary file of your own.
py.u09.learn: with open("notes.txt") as f: opens a file and closes it again when the block ends. f.read() gives all its text, and for line in f: goes through it a line at a time, each line still ending in its newline.
py.u09.detail: open("log.txt", "w") opens a file for writing and wipes what was there; "a" adds to the end instead. f.write("text\n") writes text, and the newline is yours to add. line.strip() removes the newline and any spaces at each end. Files here are temporary: they exist only while your program runs.
py.u09.example:
# Read the quest log, then add to it
with open("quests.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print("-", line.strip())

with open("quests.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Rest at the inn\n")

with open("quests.txt") as f:
    print(len(f.readlines()), "quests now")
py.u09.exampleOutput:
- Find the key
- Cross the river
- Open the gate
4 quests now
py.u09.exampleNote: strip() takes the newline off each line before printing. "a" added a fourth quest at the end, and reading the file again counts it.
py.u09.question: What would the last line say if the second open() used "w" instead of "a"?
py.u09.why: "w" wipes the file before writing, so only the new quest is left in it.
py.u09.guided: Predict, then run: change "a" to "w". Then print each line without strip(), and look at the gaps that appear.

Read the file and print three lines: how many scores there are, the highest score, and the total. Then write the total, on a line of its own, into a new file called summary.txt, and print what summary.txt holds, read back from the file.

Keep the scores in a list as whole numbers, then len(), max() and sum() do the rest. Open summary.txt with "w", write the total and a newline, then read it back in a second with block.
With other names: with open("names.txt") as f: then for row in f: and name = row.strip() inside the loop.

Make the list of scores before the loop that fills it, and spell it the same way every time.
int() could not read a line. A blank line, or one holding only spaces, has to be skipped before int().
f.write() takes text: turn the total into text with str() first.
With 10, 40 and 25 in the file, the lines are 3, 40, 75, and 75 again, read back from summary.txt.
Blank lines are not scores: skip them, and count only the lines with a number.
A file with one score and no newline at the end still has one score.
