py.u09.title: Save the game
py.u09.description: Load the hero's saved game, add what they found, and save it again, ready for next time.
py.u09.learnTitle: Save lists and dictionaries as text
py.u09.learn: json.dumps(state) turns a dictionary or a list into text, and json.loads(text) turns that text back. json.dump(state, f) and json.load(f) do the same, straight into and out of a file.
py.u09.detail: JSON holds dictionaries with text keys, lists, text, numbers, True, False and None. A set or a date cannot be saved as it is: turn it into a list or text first. JSON writes True as true and None as null, and every key comes back as text, even one that was a number.
py.u09.example:
import json
state = {"hero": "Nova", "level": 3, "pack": ["rope", "map"], "boss_beaten": False}
text = json.dumps(state)
print(text)
loaded = json.loads(text)
print(loaded["pack"][1])
print(json.dumps({1: "one"}))
py.u09.exampleNote: The text looks almost like Python, but False is written false. Loading it gives a dictionary again, so loaded["pack"][1] is map. The key 1 became the text "1".
py.u09.question: What would json.dumps({"lit": True}) give?
py.u09.why: JSON spells it true, in lowercase, without quotes. json.loads() turns it back into Python's True.
py.u09.guided: Predict, then run: add "seen": {"hall"} to the state and read the error. Then save it as a sorted list instead.
py.u09.starter: # Load save.json, update it, and save it again
py.u09.challenge: A saved game is in save.json: a dictionary with the hero's name, their gold (a whole number) and a list of items. Load it. Then ask for an item the hero found, and how much gold they found with it. Add the item to the end of the list, unless it is already there, and add the gold. Save the new state back to save.json with json.dump(), then print the file's text, read back from save.json.

py.u09.title: The score table
py.u09.concept: csv · tables in a text file
py.u09.description: Read the tournament's results table, add up each team's points, and find the top player.
py.u09.learnTitle: Rows and columns in a text file
py.u09.learn: A CSV file holds a table: one row per line, values separated by commas, usually with a header row of column names first. csv.DictReader(f) reads each row as a dictionary keyed by those names.
py.u09.detail: Every value comes back as text, so turn numbers into numbers with int() or float(). A value that contains a comma is written in quotes, "like, this", and the csv module handles it for you, which splitting on commas by hand gets wrong. csv.writer(f).writerow([...]) writes a row. Open CSV files with newline="", as the csv module asks.
py.u09.example:
import csv

    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        print(row["name"], int(row["score"]) * 2)
with open("scores.csv") as f:

Kai, the brave 110
['"Kai', ' the brave"', '55\n']

py.u09.description: Load the game's settings even when the file is missing or damaged, and say what was skipped.

py.u09.learn: Real files go missing and get damaged. Opening a file that does not exist raises a FileNotFoundError, and a line that int() cannot read raises a ValueError. Catch each one where it happens, and decide what the program should do instead.

py.u10.title: Clean up the answers
py.u10.description: Check the riddle keeper's answers fairly, whatever capitals and spaces the player types, and tidy them for display.
py.u10.learnTitle: Tools that come with every piece of text
py.u10.learn: Text has methods of its own: " Nova ".strip() is "Nova", "nova".upper() is "NOVA", and "a,b".split(",") is ["a", "b"]. A method never changes the text itself, because text cannot be changed: store what it gives back.
py.u10.detail: "a b".replace(" ", "") is "ab": replace() swaps every copy of one piece of text for another. "nOVA".capitalize() is "Nova", a capital first letter and the rest lowercase; title() does that to every word. split() with nothing in the brackets splits on any run of spaces, and " ".join(words) joins a list of words back with single spaces. f"{price:.2f}" shows a number with two decimal places.
py.u10.example:
answer = "  The Moon "
clean = answer.strip().lower()
print(clean)
print(clean == "the moon")
print("map,rope,lamp".split(","))
print(" + ".join(["rope", "map"]))
print(f"{clean.title()} costs {2.5:.2f} coins")
py.u10.exampleOutput:
the moon
True
['map', 'rope', 'lamp']
rope + map
The Moon costs 2.50 coins
py.u10.exampleNote: strip() and lower() tidy the reply before comparing it. split() makes a list, join() makes text again, and :.2f in the f-string writes 2.5 as 2.50.
py.u10.question: After name = "nova", with name.upper() on a line of its own, what does print(name) show?
py.u10.why: upper() gives back a new piece of text, which nothing stored. name still holds "nova".
py.u10.guided: Predict, then run: try " ".join(clean.split()) on "  lots   of   space ". Then change :.2f to :.1f.

py.u10.title: Spot the ticket code
py.u10.description: Recognise ticket codes in the messages that come in, whether a whole message is one or it hides inside other text.
py.u10.learn: import re, then re.search(r"\d+", text) finds the first run of digits in text, or gives None if there is none. A pattern describes a shape: \d is a digit, \w a letter, digit or _, \s a space, [A-Z] a capital letter, and . any character.
py.u10.detail: + means one or more, * zero or more, ? zero or one, and {3} exactly three. re.fullmatch() checks that the whole text has the shape, re.search() looks for it anywhere, and re.match() only at the start. Write patterns as r"..." so Python leaves the backslashes for re. .group() gives the text that matched.
py.u10.example:
import re
note = "Gate 12 opens at 7 for room B42"
print(re.search(r"\d+", note).group())
print(re.findall(r"\d+", note))
print(re.fullmatch(r"[A-Z]\d+", "B42") is not None)
print(re.search(r"x", note))
py.u10.exampleNote: \d+ takes as many digits as it can, so it finds 12, not 1. findall() gives every match. fullmatch() says B42 is a capital letter and digits, and a search that finds nothing gives None.
py.u10.question: What does re.search(r"\d+", "room 305").group() give?
py.u10.why: + means one or more, and it takes as many as it can: all three digits.
py.u10.guided: Predict, then run: try re.fullmatch on "B42!" and on "b42". Then change the pattern to [A-Za-z] and try "b42" again.
py.u10.starter: # Import re, then check each line
py.u10.challenge: A ticket code is two capital letters, a dash, and three digits, like AB-123. Ask how many lines of text there are, then read each line. For each line, print yes if the whole line is a ticket code, or no if not. On the last line, print how many of the lines had a ticket code somewhere in them, even with other text around it.
hints: The shape of a code is [A-Z]{2}, a dash, then \d{3}. fullmatch() asks whether the whole line is that shape.
search() looks for the shape anywhere in the line, which is what the count needs. match() is not enough for either job: it only looks at the start.
With other names: re.fullmatch(r"\d{4}", pin) checks a whole PIN, and re.search(r"\d{4}", note) finds one inside a note.

errorHints.text: re is a name only after import re at the top.
range() needs a whole number: use int() on the number of lines.
search() and fullmatch() give None when nothing matches, and None has no .group(). Check the result with if before using it.
AB-123 is a code; ab-123 is not, because the letters must be capitals; and Gate CD-404 now holds a code inside it, so the count is 2.
XYZ-123 is not a code as a whole line, but YZ-123 is inside it, so it counts as holding one.
A single line that is exactly a code: yes, and a count of 1.
Check lines that nearly match: an extra digit, spaces at the start, an underscore instead of a dash.
Check empty lines: no code, and a count of 0.

py.u10.title: Read the message log
py.u10.description: Pull the time and the speaker out of each message, then print the log again with every time hidden.
py.u10.learn: Brackets in a pattern make a group: re.search(r"(\d+)-(\d+)", "score 7-3") matches, and .group(1) is "7" and .group(2) is "3". re.findall() with groups gives a list of tuples, one tuple per match.
py.u10.detail: re.sub(pattern, new, text) replaces every match: re.sub(r"\d", "#", "pin 4071") gives "pin ####". Groups are numbered from 1 by their opening bracket, left to right, and group(0) is the whole match. re.match() looks only at the start of the text.
py.u10.example:
import re

for name, ours, theirs in re.findall(r"(\w+) scored (\d+)-(\d+)", log):
    print(name, int(ours) - int(theirs))
print(re.sub(r"\d", "#", "pin 4071"))
m = re.search(r"(\d+)-(\d+)", log)
print(m.group(0), m.group(2))
py.u10.exampleNote: findall() gives one tuple per match, which the for loop unpacks into three names. sub() replaces every digit. group(0) is the whole match, and group(2) the second bracket.

py.u10.title: Check the form

py.u10.description: Check usernames and times on the sign-up form: the right shape first, then values that make sense.
py.u10.learnTitle: Check the shape, not the truth
py.u10.learn: re.fullmatch() checks that a whole reply has the right shape: r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}" for a date like 2026-03-01. But the right shape is not the same as a real value: 2026-13-45 has the shape, and is no date at all.
py.u10.detail: So check the shape with a pattern, then check the meaning with code: turn the parts into numbers and test their ranges, or let a library such as datetime decide. Real email addresses are too varied for a short pattern. One @ with text on both sides is a fair first check, and the only real test is sending a message.

py.u10.question: Does re.fullmatch(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}", "2026-02-30") match?
py.u10.why: A pattern only sees digits and dashes. Knowing February has no 30th takes code that understands dates.

For a time, fullmatch() with two groups checks the shape. Then turn each group into a number and check its range, and return the answer as True or False.

A name must start with a letter, so 7nova is refused.
23:59 is the last minute of the day: True.

def valid_plate(plate):

py.u11.title: Make a hero
py.u11.description: Design a Hero blueprint once, then make a whole party of heroes from it.
py.u11.learnTitle: A blueprint for things that belong together
py.u11.learn: class Hero: starts a blueprint. Its __init__(self, name) method runs whenever a hero is made with Hero("Nova"), and self.name = name stores the name on that hero. Every object made from the class has its own attributes.
py.u11.detail: self is the object being made or used. Python passes it in for you, so Hero("Nova") has one argument while __init__ has two parameters. Read an attribute with a dot: nova.name. Forgetting self. makes a plain local name that vanishes when __init__ ends.
py.u11.example:
class Hero:
    def __init__(self, name, health=10):
        self.name = name
        self.health = health

nova = Hero("Nova")
kai = Hero("Kai", 12)
kai.health = kai.health - 3
print(nova.name, nova.health)
print(kai.name, kai.health)
py.u11.exampleNote: Each Hero() call makes a separate object. Nova uses the default health, Kai gets 12, and changing kai.health leaves Nova alone.
py.u11.question: If __init__ said health = health instead of self.health = health, what would nova.health do?
py.u11.why: Without self., health is only a local name inside __init__. The object never gets a health attribute, so asking for one is an AttributeError.
py.u11.guided: Predict, then run: take self. off the health line and read the error. Then give Hero a third attribute, level, that always starts at 1.

py.u11.title: Potions and blows
py.u11.description: Give the hero actions of their own, and keep the rules for health and potions inside the class.
py.u11.learnTitle: Give objects things they can do
py.u11.learn: A method is a function inside a class. def heal(self, amount): with self.health = self.health + amount inside changes that hero's own health. nova.heal(3) calls it, and Python passes nova in as self.
py.u11.detail: Methods keep the rules in one place: take_hit() can make sure health never goes below 0, wherever a hit comes from. Each object keeps its own state, so healing Nova leaves Kai alone. A method can also answer a question by returning a value, like is_alive().
py.u11.example:
class Hero:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.health = 10

    def take_hit(self, damage):
        self.health = max(0, self.health - damage)

    def is_alive(self):
        return self.health > 0

nova = Hero("Nova")
kai = Hero("Kai")
nova.take_hit(4)
kai.take_hit(15)
print(nova.health, nova.is_alive())
print(kai.health, kai.is_alive())
py.u11.exampleNote: Both heroes run the same take_hit(), but each changes only its own health. Kai's 15 damage stops at 0, because the rule lives in the method.
py.u11.question: Just after nova.take_hit(4), before Kai is hit, what is kai.health?
py.u11.why: Nova and Kai are separate objects with their own health. Hitting Nova changes nothing about Kai.
py.u11.guided: Predict, then run: add a heal(amount) method that never goes above 10, and heal Nova by 7. Then check kai.is_alive() after healing Nova.

py.u11.title: A hero with a pack
py.u11.description: Build the hero from smaller parts: a pack with a weight limit, holding items, each class doing one job.
py.u11.learn: A hero can have a pack, and a pack can hold items. Give Hero an attribute self.pack = Pack(), and the hero can ask the pack to do its part: hero.pack.add(rope). This is composition: each class does one job, and together they make something bigger.
py.u11.detail: Reach for composition before inheritance, class Wizard(Hero):, which is for an "is a kind of" link. A hero is not a kind of pack; a hero has a pack. Make each pack inside __init__, so that every hero gets a pack of their own.

map True
lamp False
Nova ['rope', 'map']
py.u11.exampleNote: The hero's pack is its own object, with its own limit and list. The third item doesn't fit, so add() says False and leaves the pack as it was.
py.u11.question: If pack = Pack(2) were written in the class body instead of in __init__, what would two heroes share?
py.u11.why: A value in the class body is made once, for the whole class, so every hero would point at that one pack.
py.u11.guided: Predict, then run: make a second hero, add an item to their pack, and check that Nova's pack is unchanged. Then give Pack a method count() that returns how many items it holds.

Pack has a weight limit, a list of items, a method weight() that returns the total weight of its items, and a method add(item) that adds the item and returns True only if the total stays within the limit, and otherwise returns False and changes nothing. Hero has a name and a pack whose limit is the hero's strength. Ask for the hero's name and strength, then how many items there are, then each item's name and weight, all weights being whole numbers. Try to add each item to the hero's pack, and print its name and added, or its name and too heavy. Then print the hero's name, carries, and the pack's weight, like Nova carries 5, and on the last line the names of the items in the pack, joined with a comma and a space, or nothing if it is empty.
hints: Write Item first, then Pack, then Hero, and test each alone. Hero's __init__ makes a Pack with the strength as its limit.
add() works out what the weight would be with the new item, before adding it. The program never checks weights itself: it asks the hero's pack.
